news.title: Democratic voters reject Resistance stars
news.text:
Conway ran in New York’s 12th Congressional District, in Manhattan, the seat vacated by the retirement of Democratic Rep. Jerry Nadler. There were a lot of candidates. Conway finished fifth, with 6.1% of the vote. A wealthy lawyer, Conway loaned his campaign $2 million for the run. In all, he spent $5.7 million.

The money allowed Conway to mount a vanity campaign, to publicly fantasize about getting Trump, and to pound his chest about the massive damage judgment against Trump in the Carroll trial. “Hi, Donald! It’s me, George Conway,” began one ad. “I cost you $88 million f***ing dollars, and I’ve only just gotten started.” For his next act, Conway promised to put Trump in jail.

Conway obviously thought the theme might work in New York’s 12th, in which Kamala Harris beat Trump 81% to 17% in the 2024 presidential election. But of course all Democrats in the race promised to oppose Trump. The Democratic voters’ job was to choose the best. Conway was not their first, or their second, or their third, or their fourth choice. Instead, the primary winner was a member of the New York state Assembly named Micah C. Lasher, who pledged to stand up to Trump.

The other Resistance star to face-plant was Alexander Vindman, who in 2019, as an active-duty Army lieutenant colonel on the staff of the National Security Council, set in motion the first impeachment of Trump. Vindman, who was privy to some of the president’s calls with world leaders, felt that Trump had committed some sort of unspecified violation in a conversation with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Vindman relayed secret information to a friend in the CIA, who came up with a “whistleblower” complaint against the president.

The idea of a whistleblower complaint was preposterous because “there was no scenario in which the president, as head of the executive branch, was covered by any whistleblower law.” (The line is from my book Obsession, which delved into the first-term efforts to remove Trump.) There was simply no provision in the law that would allow it. But Congress can do what it wants, and Democrats, who controlled the House and were frustrated by the recent collapse of the Russia investigation, adopted Vindman’s cause. The impeachment went on.

Vindman testified in private and in public but refused to detail precisely how he got the impeachment ball rolling. Democrats defended him and pushed back against Republicans who sought to know to whom Vindman had given the story of the Trump-Zelensky call. “All the facts point that Vindman here is the coefficient, that he sparked this whole thing,” said a senior Republican aide involved in the impeachment. “For all intents and purposes, Vindman is the whistleblower here, but he was able to get somebody else to do his dirty work for him.”

The impeachment failed, of course. Under pressure from the Trump administration, Vindman retired from the military and began trading on his notoriety. He wrote a memoir called Here, Right Matters, with the title based on his congressional testimony. He started a company called Here Right Matters LLC. It did well; in a financial disclosure form this year, Vindman listed around $1.5 million in income from that and other ventures. The Alexander Vindman business did pretty well.

The next step would be politics. Vindman moved to Florida and ran for the Senate as a Democrat. When he jumped into the race in January, his announcement video began with news clips from his role in the Trump impeachment. A moment later, Vindman said, as pictures of his congressional testimony played: “The last time you saw me was here, swearing an oath to tell the truth about a president who broke his. See, my family came to America as refugees to escape tyranny. And I sure as hell was not going to bow down to some wannabe tyrant. This president unleashed a reign of terror and retribution, not just against me and my family, but against all of us.”

No subtlety there; the Hero of the Resistance had arrived to take on Donald Trump! Vindman raised $16 million for his campaign, while his socialist opponent, Angie Nixon, raised a little less than $1 million. Vindman immediately became a heavy favorite to win the Democratic nomination. He remained the favorite until Election Day, when Nixon shocked the political world by trouncing Vindman, 56% to 44%.

Once again, the Resistance 1.0 magic did not work. As it had been in Manhattan, only on a far larger scale, Florida Democratic voters just didn’t care that a candidate had led one of the many unsuccessful efforts to drive Trump out of office from 2017 to 2021. That doesn’t mean they like or support Trump; they absolutely don’t. But it does mean that all the excitement that George Conway and Alexander Vindman and their allies stirred up in the wayback time of Trump I truly came to nothing.

news.title: Iran, the economy and mending fences: Top takeaways from Trump interview with friend-turned-foe Michael Cohen
news.text:
Donald Trump and Michael Cohen discussed Iran, the economy, immigration and their own repaired relationship in a newly released WABC radio interview.

Cohen shared an excerpt Thursday from his first public conversation with Trump in eight years. The former Trump lawyer described the exchange as “easy” and “familiar” after a bitter split that defined much of Trump’s first term.

The president used the interview to defend his ongoing war with Iran, claiming the country’s military and leadership had been severely weakened. He also repeated his longstanding pledge that Iran cannot be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.

Trump further called the U.S. economy a “renaissance,” boasted about his record on illegal immigration and even claimed that he would win by 25 points if he were to run for reelection — despite polls indicating his approval rating remains at historic lows.

The interview was notable for the participants as much as its substance. Cohen was once Trump’s fiercely loyal fixer before becoming a key witness against him. The two have recently resumed contact, with Cohen describing their reconciliation as having been rooted in a shared sense of betrayal.

Cohen opened the interview by acknowledging the men’s checkered history. “You and I have obviously traveled a pretty rocky road together,” he told Trump, who called in over the phone.

Trump responded sympathetically, saying, “They weaponized you like nobody’s ever been weaponized.” He also praised Cohen for having “recanted everything you said,” apparently referring to Cohen’s January claim that New York officials had pressured him to testify against Trump.

Cohen served for years as Trump’s personal attorney, even claiming he would “take a bullet” for him. But their relationship collapsed after Cohen called Trump a “con man” in 2019 and later testified against Trump in his New York hush money trial.

Cohen, who served three years in prison for lying to Congress and tax violations, became an outspoken Trump critic – one whom Democrats embraced. In 2024, for instance, he claimed Trump would run the U.S. “like the Führer” if re-elected. The president branded him a “sleazebag.”

This summer, however, Cohen said the two had rekindled their relationship due to a “shared experience of betrayal.” He said that after criticizing New York Democrats and saying he had never seen Trump meet with Jeffrey Epstein, the pair reconnected. “The ice between us, it didn’t just melt, it broke,” he told WABC in July.

Cohen also said Thursday that he had submitted a pardon application to the White House.

During the interview excerpt, Trump characterized Iran as militarily weakened and economically strained, while arguing that continued U.S. pressure remains necessary.

“We’re doing very well with Iran,” Trump said. “The navy’s gone, the air force is gone, the leadership is gone.” He said the loss of Iranian leaders had also complicated diplomacy because “nobody knows who’s leading.”

Trump argued — as he long has — that the central issue was preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. “Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” he said. “Very simple.”

Still, the president acknowledged the ongoing war could increase energy and gasoline costs, but argued that such consequences were necessary. 

“We’ve wiped them out militarily,” Trump said, while conceding that Iran still has missiles and drones. He said he would have made the same decision “100 times” because, in his view, Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon, and they won’t be having a nuclear weapon.”

Trump further claimed that, without him, much of the Middle East would be destroyed.

“There would be no Israel if there was not a Donald Trump president,” he told Cohen. “I think there'd be no Saudi Arabia either. Right now, I believe the Middle East would have been entirely wiped out.”

Multiple polls indicate a majority of Americans are opposed to the Iran war, which has now dragged on for nearly five months, upending the global energy industry. To date, 18 US service members have been killed in the war, and hundreds more have been wounded.

Elsewhere in the interview, the president called the U.S. economy a “renaissance.”

“There’s never been anything like it,” Trump said. “We had the greatest economy ever in my first term. This is going to blow it away.”

He focused on semiconductor production, saying the U.S. had become too dependent on imports from Taiwan. Trump said massive chip plants are now being built, including in Arizona, and that the country would no longer need to import the technology.

Trump also pointed to pharmaceutical manufacturing, arguing that the Covid-19 pandemic exposed U.S. dependence on foreign countries for medicine and medical equipment.

“Medicine is coming back,” Trump said. “We learned that from Covid because we didn’t make medicine.”

He named Eli Lilly, Merck and Pfizer among companies expanding U.S. operations, and argued that his sweeping tariffs — struck down by the Supreme Court in February — were driving companies to build factories domestically.

As with Iran, Americans appear to be at odds with the president on the economy. A recent Financial Times survey found that a majority of respondents believe economic conditions have worsened under Trump.

Trump said he had immediately resolved what he described as an uncontrollable situation at the U.S.-Mexico border, and complained that the achievement had received too little attention.

“When I came in, the border — they would allow 25 million people,” Trump said.

“I solved the problem in 30 days and solved it beautifully in 60,” Trump said. He claimed that “zero people came in” through the southern border in the past 16 months. U.S. Customs and Border Protection recently said that zero releases had occurred at the border in 15 months.

Trump also criticized former Vice President Kamala Harris, saying she had failed to engage with Border Patrol officials. He argued that border security helped him win in 2016 and remained a central political issue in later campaigns.

“A victory has a two-week life,” Trump said, suggesting voters had moved on from an issue that he said had once dominated public discourse.

According to an August YouGov poll, 53 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump’s handling of immigration, while 40 percent approve. By comparison, at the start of Trump’s term, 51 percent approved and 40 percent disapproved.
news.summary: Michael Cohen, Trump’s former fixer turned key witness against him, said it was their first public conversation in eight years

news.title: Aisha Wahab Wins Special Election to Succeed Former California Rep. Eric Swalwell
news.text:
California state Sen. Aisha Wahab won the Aug. 18 special election in the state’s 14th Congressional District to serve the remainder of U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term.

Wahab also placed first in the June 2 primary.

While Wahab has finished first in polling results, Hernandez outraised Wahab by more than $902,514. Hernandez had more cash on hand than Wahab by just over $29,230.

There was outside spending in the race including by United Democracy Project, a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee that spent $1.2 million on the special election in support of Hernandez and in opposition to Wahab. Another super PAC, Bold America, spent $664,921 in support of Hernandez.

Altogether, outside groups spent about $4.1 million on the special election since mid-July. About $3.7 million was spent in support of Hernandez, while about $400,000 backed Wahab.

Wahab campaigned on banning junk fees nationwide, building more housing at all income levels, banning congressional stock trading, supporting small businesses, and protecting abortion rights.

The 14th Congressional District was affected by mid-decade redistricting last year. The new map will take effect for the full term, which begins in January. Therefore, the winner of the special election will serve under the current boundaries until then. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the current district with 65.8 percent of the vote in the 2024 presidential election. Under the new map, she would have won with 65.4 percent.

Swalwell served in Congress from January 2013 until his April 2026 retirement. The allegations prompted him to also withdraw from the California gubernatorial race following pressure from fellow Democrats including Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

“I am deeply sorry to my family, staff, and constituents for mistakes in judgment I’ve made in my past,” Swalwell wrote in a post on X. “I will fight the serious, false allegation made against me. However, I must take responsibility and ownership for the mistakes I did make.”

news.title: Second polling firm admits to fabricating data after fake survey rocks LA mayor’s race
news.text:
A second polling firm is under fire after admitting to fabricating data in a key 2026 primary election, this time in Florida.

The polling monitor FiftyPlusOne wrote in a blog post on Thursday that it had received a tip suggesting that pollster The Public Sentiment Institute (TPSI) had violated one of its rules by not disclosing publicly that a survey it had released of the Republican gubernatorial primary field was commissioned by one of the candidates — a disclosure pollsters are required to make by most polling aggregators to be considered legitimate firms, as campaign-sponsored polls often tilt in the favor of the relevant candidates.

But in the course of investigating that tip, FiftyPlusOne says its analysts discovered a second problem — that a TPSI poll postmortem published in the wake of the Florida primary election on Tuesday admitted TPSI pollsters had changed the results of some respondents’ answers to lean towards James Fishback, the candidate who’d sponsored the poll. Fishback went on to be defeated in Tuesday’s primary, placing third behind Jay Collins and the winner, Rep. Byron Donalds.

“Jay Collins was polling in the twenties in our data. That did not align with our read of the race, and we concluded it might reflect a data-quality problem specific to our text-message panel. Acting on that conclusion, we identified respondents who selected Collins but whose broader profile aligned with a competing coalition, and leaned those respondents toward James Fishback,” read TPSI’s postmortem.

FiftyPlusOne called the admission evidence of an “obvious violation of standard polling practices,” which it said was “made all the more questionable by the undisclosed relationship between the pollster and the Fishback campaign.” The polling aggregator said it would not use TPSI polls in its analytics in the future.

The admission from TPSI is one that will further challenge trust in polling firms and election analytics at a moment when that trust is already badly shaken. The news comes just days after a group calling itself “Median Strategies” announced that it was shutting down after publishing fake poll results in the Los Angeles mayoral race as part of a “social experiment”.

“All previously published polling releases have been withdrawn and should not be cited or treated as genuine polling data. Median Strategies was created as a short-term social experiment examining how purported polling information could enter and spread through the political information ecosystem without independent verification,” read the group’s statement. A 21-year-old recent college graduate was revealed by The Guardian as the owner of the site and fake company, whose “polls” were shared widely online after they showed two candidates in two separate races leading their opponents by wide margins.

“I wanted to see if fake polls could really penetrate the ecosystem that easily,” Rahil Prakash said in an interview with The Guardian, adding: “And as it turned out, it could.” 

Prakash’s fake polling data gave fans of Francesca Hong undue confidence ahead of her defeat in last week’s Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, and was even cited by the campaign of Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass as she runs for re-election against progressive Nithya Raman. They were not picked up by credible polling aggregators, but the two polls spread quickly online anyway.

And the 2026 cycle follows an embarrassing cycle for legitimate pollsters; the 2024 presidential election was capped off by a poll by much-cited Iowa polling guru Ann Selzer which showed Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris in the lead in Iowa with only days to go before the election. Harris went on to lose not just Iowa but every other major battleground state in her matchup with Donald Trump, and Selzer retired from political polling. She insisted afterwards that her decision was not related to the serious discrepancy between her final poll and the election results.

Polling this cycle looks to be little better. In Michigan, the industry’s collective margin of error in the highly-watched Democratic primary for U.S. Senate was more than 10 points, according to an analysis from local newscaster WLNS 6. 

Though Prakash didn’t draw a conclusion from the results of his “social experiment”, it’s safe to say that the trust issues surrounding political polling in the U.S. will only be made worse by further admissions like the ones this week from TPSI.
news.summary: Pollster TPSI admits it changed responses from voters supporting Jay Collins to indicate greater support for James Fishback

news.title: Progressives notch victory in race to replace Swalwell following sexual assault scandal
news.text: Progressive state Sen. and Assistant Majority Leader Aisha Wahab has bested Melissa Hernandez, a more moderate public transit executive, in a special election to replace disgraced Rep. Eric Swalwell. The race between Wahab and Hernandez represented another front in the Democratic civil war between the party’s establishment and progressive wings. Wahab counted on high-profile endorsements from California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis and labor icon Dolores Huerta, while Hernandez relied on large sums of super PAC cash and endorsements from local officials. PRIMARY TAKEAWAYS: DEMS’ LEFT-CENTER BATTLE INTENSIFIES AS SCHUMER TAKES ANOTHER HIT; SPLIT DECISION FOR TRUMP While progressive Democrats opened the election season strongly, securing high-profile victories in New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado and D.C., they have more recently underperformed on expectations in the Democratic primaries for Michigan’s Senate race and Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race. Wahab was the strong favorite heading into Election Day, earning 42.8% of the vote in the special primary against Hernandez’s 16.8%. California has "jungle primaries" in which the top two vote-getters, regardless of party affiliation, advance to the general election. Wahab and Hernandez, both Democrats, occupied the top two slots in the special primary, effectively shutting Republicans out of a district that Kamala Harris carried easily in the 2024 presidential election. The special election, however, represents only a temporary victory because it determined who would serve out the remaining two months of Swalwell’s term. Examining Harp's influence is fair game. Turning a female White House aide into a breathless story about the older president and the younger, attractive blonde beside him is something else.

From the Daily Beast:

Trump was forced to address the issue on Monday after Democratic rising star Jon Ossoff publicly questioned the president’s closeness with his 35-year-old executive assistant, declaring at a rally that Trump would much rather “travel with Natalie” and build the White House ballroom than do his job as president.Asked in the Oval office about Ossoff’s comments, Trump hit back at the Georgia senator, who is up for re-election in November, before immediately reverting to a lengthy rant about his pet vanity project.“You mean Pee-wee Herman? (He’s a) Pee-wee Herman look-alike,” the president said, referencing the nickname he has given to Ossoff.The comments are the first time Trump has been asked publicly about Harp, who has become an ever-present figure in his orbit.In recent weeks, she has been photographed alongside him at Camp David, spotted next to him at his Bedminister Golf Club, and has been seen watching on adoringly as Trump signed an executive order in the Oval Office requiring childhood vaccine shots to be spaced out.

This from Vanity Fair:

Donald Trump, president of the United States and notorious bottle blond, has long been known for his capriciousness when it comes to those he surrounds himself with, able to do 180s on folks who were once trusted colleagues and turn them into video game foes (just look at Michaels Pence, Cohen, and Flynn, to name a few). There’s one peroxide blowout, however, who’s consistently been spotted at Trump’s side, often clutching a disheveled stack of printouts, since 2022: Natalie Harp.Harp currently holds the dual roles of special assistant and executive assistant to the president. She reportedly sits at a desk just outside the Oval Office; pulls in a taxpayer-funded $150,000 annual salary; has unmatched access to Trump; is responsible for posting his Truth Social missives; travels alongside the president (including during his recent secret airplane switcheroo exodus from Turkey); fields texts from world leaders; and more. Harp even celebrated her 35th birthday earlier this month at Trump’s side: That’s her in the background of the fourth photo in Lara Trump’s Instagram post, ringing in her mid-30s at Trump’s Bedminster golf club.In All or Nothing, Michael Wolff’s chronicle of the 2024 election, Wolff revealed Harp’s duty as the keeper of the “good-news printer,” with the aide toting a wireless printer to conjure printouts of news articles and emails to hand to Trump for his satisfaction, validation, and jubilation.

Now, let's change the uniform.

Former Vice President and presidential candidate Kamala "Kackles" Harris dated former San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown in 1994 and 1995, when Brown was California Assembly speaker. Brown appointed Harris to two state boards.

Those are facts.

Harris had already worked as a prosecutor; their relationship ended years before she won her first election, and claims that she simply slept her way into political power went beyond what the evidence established.

When the conservative media turned Harris's relationship with Brown into sexual jokes and suggestions that sex explained her political rise, the political press knew exactly where the whistle was. The attacks were described as sexist, sexualized, demeaning, and out of bounds.

From FactCheck.org:

Harris was 29 in March 1994 when a San Francisco Chronicle columnist described her as Brown’s “new steady,” going on to say that she was “something new in Willie’s love life. She’s a woman, not a girl.” At the time, Brown, who was then 60 years old and speaker of the California State Assembly, had been estranged from his wife for more than a decade.As speaker, Brown appointed Harris to the California Medical Assistance Commission later that year, which provides the basis for claims that Brown helped Harris’ career that sometimes accompany the claims suggesting that she broke up his marriage. (Brown left the Assembly in 1995, and became mayor of San Francisco until 2004.)Brown had married Blanche Vitero in 1957 and the couple had three children. But by the early 1970s, Brown was frequently seen around town with young women and his marriage collapsed, according to a 1996 biography written by James Richardson, a senior writer at the Sacramento Bee. It was at this time that Brown got the first of a “series of apartments” of his own, while his “relationship with his wife settled into a mutually beneficial friendship,” Richardson wrote.A 1984 profile published in the New York Times described Brown as an “escort for attractive women” and “good friend of his former wife,” from whom it says he “separated amicably” two years earlier.“I don’t know whether the marriage failed and the relationship survived or vice versa, but something very valuable lasted,” Brown wrote in his own 2008 autobiography, explaining that he and his wife had celebrated their 50th anniversary in 2007, although they hadn’t lived together in 25 years.“Although Blanche and I led very different lives, there was never a breakup,” he wrote. “The two of us kept the family circle going. We’ve always been in each other’s lives. We’re friends.”

Some Republicans even warned their own side to knock it off.

That standard wasn't unreasonable; a woman's relationship with a powerful man doesn't prove that her career is sexual currency.

So apply it.

Harp's access to Trump is newsworthy; her ability to put information in front of the president is newsworthy; her role in his social media operation, her travel with him, and the influence she may have inside the White House are all legitimate subjects.

Her blonde hair isn't.

Neither are her shoes, her age beside Trump's age, her battle with cancer, or headlines calling her his "companion" while inviting readers and viewers to speculate about a relationship for which no evidence has been presented.

Ossoff later called Harp a "security blanket" and argued that Trump surrounds himself with aides who tell him what he wants to hear. 

Fine. Make that argument, challenge her influence, challenge her judgment, or challenge her work.

But don't spend two years telling America that sexualizing Harris is misogyny, then discover the entertainment value of a 35-year-old blonde when she works for Trump.

The Referee Test isn't complicated: if gendered innuendo deserves a whistle, blow it regardless of which team has the ball.

Same innuendo, different woman, different whistle.

And the referee fails again.

news.title: What’s animating undecided voters in two key states: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman share their observations from our latest round of voter focus groups. Plus, we dive into the role Joe Biden and Kamala Harris are playing in the midterms. Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here. — Adam Wollner Focus groups: Deep anxiety about the economy drives undecided voters in two key Senate races By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Concerns about the economy and high costs are driving the thinking of undecided voters in Iowa and Georgia, according to new focus group conversations, as two states that will be central to the fight for the Senate barrel toward Election Day.“Nothing has gotten better as far as the cost of living, inflation — food is astronomical, gas,” said Patty O., a 59-year-old Georgia Republican who voted for Donald Trump in 2024. “The cost of living is so high right now.” Patty was among a dozen voters up for grabs in two Senate races who participated this week in focus groups produced by Syracuse University and the research firms Engagious and Sago and observed by NBC News. The group comprised six independents, five Republicans and one Democrat. Nine voted for Trump for president two years ago, when he won both states, while three supported then-Vice President Kamala Harris. All but three of the voters said they feel more anxious about the economy today than when Trump returned to office. Eight said Trump is not focused enough on the issue. “Among these undecided voters, pervasive economic anxiety is the animating issue in the midterms — not Iran, not immigration, not Israel/Gaza,” said Rich Thau of Engagious, who moderated the sessions. Overall, eight of the 12 undecided voters said they disapproved of Trump’s job performance during his second term, even though a majority of the disapprovers voted for him in 2024. Jamie G., a 55-year-old Iowa independent who voted for Trump, said he is “disillusioned with pretty much everything he’s done since he took office.” “He was going to end conflicts on the first day, which he didn’t do. Instead, he’s gotten us into needless wars. His tariffs have caused prices — it’s been like a tax on things for the American people,” he said. “He’s more worried about his vanity projects, like the reflecting pool and his ballroom, than he is with the real problems in this country,” he added. While these voters were undecided in their state’s Senate races, some had made up their minds in the gubernatorial elections. Four of the five Iowa panelists said they would support Democrat Rob Sand. And in Georgia, three said they would vote for Republican Rick Jackson. Read more → Biden and Harris return to the campaign airwaves By Adam Wollner Joe Biden and Kamala Harris are back on the airwaves — this time in a crowded Democratic House primary in Massachusetts. Dan Koh, a former Biden White House official, began running an ad recently that features the former president and vice president speaking directly to camera in support of his campaign. Koh points to his time in the administration, saying he’s “the only candidate with the experience to take on Trump.” He’s one of a half dozen Democrats running in the deep-blue 6th District to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, who is challenging Sen. Ed Markey. “Let’s go Dan Koh,” Biden says to close out the spot. Democrats running in the midterms have generally steered clear of Biden, with wounds from the party’s 2024 defeat in the presidential election still fresh. Prior to Koh, Biden had only issued one endorsement this year: to Keisha Lance Bottoms, another former White House official who is now the Democratic nominee for governor in Georgia. Two of Biden’s Cabinet officials, former Health Secretary Xavier Becerra and former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, are on the ballot this fall for governor of California and New Mexico, respectively. As Adam Edelman reported earlier this year, Becerra rarely mentioned Biden directly on the campaign trail, while touting achievements from his time in the administration. For her part, Haaland continued to publicly praise Biden. Harris has been more involved in midterms as she weighs a 2028 presidential bid. But that hasn’t always been welcome. After Harris’ PAC sent out a fundraising email in support of former Rep. Mary Peltola, the Alaska Democratic Senate candidate distanced herself from the former vice president. Harris also notably recorded a robocall for Rep. Jasmine Crockett as she ran for the Senate in Texas earlier this year. But Crockett lost the primary to state Rep. James Talarico. 🔵 Meanwhile, in the Senate race: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., endorsed Markey, 80, over Moulton, 47, ahead of the Sept. 1 primary. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

news.title: True scale of Meghan and Harry’s US political plans revealed — from request for Biden Oval Office meeting to eyeing Senate seat
news.text:
WASHINGTON — Delusional Prince Harry and Meghan Markle sought US political clout far beyond the dreams of any British royal since King George III, The Post has learned, with the Duchess of Sussex angling to take over the Senate seat held by Kamala Harris ahead of the 2020 presidential election.

Weeks before Democrat Joe Biden’s win over President Donald Trump, a source says, Markle requested a sitdown with California Gov. Gavin Newsom because she “wanted to be considered to be appointed” to the seat held by Harris, which she vacated just before becoming vice president on Jan. 20, 2021. The source added that the discussion was publicly described as a welcome-to-California chat to head off potential inquiries.

It is unclear just how far Markle’s appeal got with Newsom, who appointed California Secretary of State Alex Padilla to replace Harris two days before her swearing-in as Biden’s second-in-command. Padilla subsequently won election to a full six-year term in 2022.

A Sussex source firmly denied that Markle wanted to take over the Harris seat, while a rep for Newsom did not respond to a request for comment.

A memorandum from Newsom’s office that surfaced in February 2021 confirmed the governor had an “introductory meeting” with the royal couple on Oct. 19, 2020, though the specific topics discussed were not disclosed and the Democrat’s team characterized it as a social occasion. It was not immediately clear whether Markle asked to meet with Newsom separately post-election.

Had the Duchess of Sussex been appointed to the world’s greatest deliberative body, the move likely would have been challenged on constitutional grounds. Article I, Section 9, Clause 8 of the founding document states that “no Person holding any Office of Profit or Trust … shall, without the Consent of the Congress, accept of any present, Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever, from any King, Prince, or foreign State.”

A British royal serving in the Senate, even a non-working one, would also have flown in the face of America’s republican tradition, as Alexander Hamilton — the founder of The Post — wrote in “The Federalist Papers” that “the importance of the prohibition of titles of nobility … [is] the corner-stone of republican government; for so long as they are excluded, there can never be serious danger that the government will be any other than that of the people.”

The ill-fated Senate maneuvering wasn’t the only time Harry and Meghan dipped their toes into US politics while trying to achieve the same prominence they enjoyed in the UK.

In late 2021, the couple requested an Oval Office meeting with Biden, as well as accommodations at nearby Blair House — a perk reserved for foreign leaders on state visits, multiple sources say.

White House staff quickly rejected the idea, with one source noting the spectacle of Harry and Meghan sitting down with the leader of the free world “would have caused a major diplomatic kerfuffle” with 10 Downing Street and the British Royal Family.

Another source, a former Biden aide, said the president and first lady Jill Biden — longstanding admirers of Queen Elizabeth II — “didn’t want to get into a family squabble” by hosting the rogue royals.

Had their pitch been successful, Harry and Meghan would have gained immeasurable prestige and stature at a time when they were struggling to find their identity following their January 2020 “Megxit” from royal duties.

To that end, the couple hired several consultants who had worked in the Barack Obama White House — including Harry’s current chief of staff Miranda Barbot — and acted as a bridge to the Biden administration, relaying the royal couple’s audacious request to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue.

Then-White House press secretary Jen Psaki, Obama’s former communications director, was one of those conduits. In her 2024 memoir “Say More,” Psaki — currently a host on left-wing cable channel MS NOW — recalled that Meghan once sent a box of lemons to Psaki’s Virginia home so she could carry them past White House security and deliver them to Jill Biden’s East Wing office.

Here’s the latest on Harry and Meghan’s move back to the UK:

King Charles only learned of Harry and Meghan’s shocking return to UK days ago

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle likely to list Montecito mansion: sources

All the signs Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have been plotting UK comeback

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s UK move is ‘huge slap in the face’ to William, creates ‘serious risks’ for monarchy

The Sussex source declined Thursday that the couple had asked for either an Oval Office meeting or to stay at Blair House, but Harry and Meghan have a history of trying to use the American presidency for PR coups.

In September 2022, the royal pair inquired whether they could hitch a ride back to the United States aboard Air Force One after the late queen’s funeral.

The request was promptly denied.

Harry and Meghan also tried to use their influence by other means.

In September 2020, the couple gave a video interview to Time magazine in which they urged Americans to vote and “reject hate speech,” which many interpreted as support for Biden. At the time, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were called out by some commentators for breaking from the British tradition that royals do not participate in party politics.

“I wish a lot of luck to Harry, because he’s going to need it,” Trump responded dismissively to the couple’s appeal.

Meghan, who retained her American citizenship even after marrying Harry in 2018, tried to make her voice heard in legislative matters as well. In November 2021, she reached out to several senators to lobby for federally mandated paid family leave.

Ultimately the couple’s attempt to become kingmakers fizzled out, similar to their ambitions in Hollywood and the lifestyle space.

Harry and Meghan even wore out their welcome with the Biden administration, sources say, despite the first couple’s personal sympathy for the prince following the loss of his mother, Princess Diana, in a 1997 car crash. Joe Biden’s first wife Neilia and infant daughter Naomi were killed in a 1972 vehicle wreck that also injured the couple’s two sons, Beau and Hunter.

Jill Biden, meanwhile, had been a regular at The Invictus Games, the sporting event for wounded warriors founded by Harry in 2014 — often appearing at the prince’s side. Jill ultimately stopped attending the games after she became first lady in January 2021, due once again to the optics surrounding Harry’s departure from the UK.
news.summary: Delusional Prince Harry and Meghan Markle sought US political clout far beyond the dreams of any British royal since King George III.

news.title: At the Races: Party’s (not) over?
news.text:
Welcome to At the Races! Each week we bring you news and analysis from the CQ Roll Call campaign team. Know someone who’d like to get this newsletter? They can subscribe here.

By Daniela Altimari and Mary Ellen McIntire

American politics is defined by partisan divides, disenfranchised voters, big money and powerful political parties.

Some advocates assert that nonpartisan primaries could solve at least some of those problems. 

Under such a system, all candidates, regardless of party affiliation, compete on the same primary ballot.

Three states currently deploy this approach. In Alaska, the top four candidates advance to the general election ballot, which is decided by ranked choice voting; while in California and Washington state, the top two primary finishers compete in November.

Voters in Massachusetts will consider a ballot question this fall that, if approved, would make the Bay State the fourth.

Supporters say nonpartisan primaries would give unaffiliated voters a greater voice in choosing candidates, which is especially important in states where one party holds most of the political leverage and primaries are, in effect, the general election. 

Such a system would foster greater competition, bolster voter turnout and dilute the power of political parties by forcing candidates to appeal to a broad swath of the electorate, not just the party base, advocates say.

Critics counter that nonpartisan primaries empower big-money interests by allowing deep-pocketed outside influencers and wealthy candidates to spend their way to the top amid crowded fields. 

And they say such a system could leave a large chunk of the electorate “orphaned” in November. That’s what happened in California this year, where general elections in several key House races are one-party affairs, including the contest for the redrawn 40th District between Republican Reps. Young Kim and Ken Calvert. 

Those arguments against nonpartisan primaries helped sink similar ballot measures in Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nevada and South Dakota in 2024.

This week’s outcome in Alaska provides more fodder for opponents of nonpartisan primaries: In a 15-candidate field for the state’s at-large House seat, the person currently in fourth place is Democrat Eric Hafner, a perennial candidate who currently resides in a federal prison in New York. According to the Anchorage Daily News, a shadowy group had spent money boosting Hafner’s candidacy. 

According to The Associated Press, Hafner had 4,954 votes with 80 percent of the vote counted, as of 8 p.m. Wednesday.

Alaska voters narrowly rejected an attempt to repeal the top-four primary system via ballot measure in 2024. They get a do-over this fall, with a similar proposal on the November ballot.

Starting gate

Florida recap: It was a busy Tuesday night in the Sunshine State, as embattled Republican Rep. Cory Mills lost his primary to former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah. President Donald Trump, who had endorsed Mills earlier this year before the congressman’s scandals gathered steam, later threw his support behind Elijah, revealing he had previously urged Mills to drop out of the race. In other key contests, state Rep. Angie Nixon scored an upset win in the Democratic Senate primary, while Democratic Reps. Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz held off primary challenges.

Cowboy State consequences: Wyoming Secretary of State Chuck Gray beat out eight competitors to win the Republican primary for the state’s at-large House seat, putting him on a glide path to succeed GOP Rep. Harriet M. Hageman, who easily won her Senate primary.

But Trump suffered a setback, with his preferred candidate for governor falling in the Republican primary.

Photos of the week: With primaries in a handful of New England states looming, Roll Call photojournalist Tom Williams recently visited Massachusetts and New Hampshire, where he caught up with Democratic candidates on the campaign trail, including stops at a “speed dating” event and a softball game. 

Third time’s a charm: Trump has returned to floating a bid for a third term, our colleague John T. Bennett reports, though he acknowledged the constitutional roadblocks in his way: “Everybody wants me to do it, but the law is very strong.”

Red to blue: The DCCC added five more candidates to its “Red to Blue” program for strong challengers: Leela Gray in Florida’s 13th District; Zach Dembo in Kentucky’s 6th; Matt Dunlap in Maine’s 2nd; Nancy Lacore in South Carolina’s 1st; and former Rep. Tom Perriello in Virginia’s 5th.

#FL09: Navy veteran Dan Green has clinched the Republican nomination for Central Florida’s 9th District. He was leading farmer Ben Butler by fewer than 600 votes with more than 95 percent of votes counted, when The Associated Press called the race Thursday. Green will face Democratic Rep. Darren Soto in a redrawn district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

#CA14: The all-Democratic special election to succeed disgraced former Rep. Eric Swalwell in California’s 14th District remains uncalled as of early Thursday afternoon. State Sen. Aisha Wahab leads Bay Area Rapid Transit Board President Melissa Hernandez 51 percent to 49 percent, with an estimated 62 percent of votes counted, the AP reported. Meanwhile, federal agents have reportedly seized electronic devices from Swalwell and searched his Washington home as part of an investigation in sexual misconduct allegations.

Show-Me the map: A Missouri judge cleared the way for the state to use its new congressional map in this year’s midterm elections, but the question of whether the map should be put to a statewide vote is likely to end up before the state Supreme Court. 

Teaming up: Pennsylvania Democrats Bob Harvie, Bob Brooks, Paige Cognetti and Janelle Stelson have announced a joint fundraising committee as they seek to flip four House seats in the battleground state this fall. 

#MASEN: New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is backing Sen. Edward J. Markey’s reelection bid, while Markey’s opponent in the Sept. 1 Democratic primary, Rep. Seth Moulton, picked up the endorsement of The Boston Globe editorial board. 

Crossing lines in California: Venture capitalist Eric Jones’ challenge to 14-term Rep. Mike Thompson, a fellow Democrat, in California’s 4th District got a boost from Republican Ray Riehle, who finished third in the June 3 all-party primary. Though they hail from different parties, Riehle shares a disdain for deeply entrenched Democrats, The (Santa Rosa) Press Democrat reported.

#MIGOV: Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, has selected state Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks as her running mate. Benson faces Republican Rep. John James, who last week also picked a state legislator as his lieutenant governor choice.

Win one, lose some: Florida Democrats who once served in Congress had mixed fortunes in their comeback bids Tuesday. Charlie Crist, the state’s former governor now running for St. Petersburg mayor, advanced to a runoff against incumbent Ken Welch. But former Rep. Stephanie Murphy came up short in her race to be the next mayor of Orange County, home to Orlando. She finished third. And former Reps. Alan Grayson, a perennial candidate, and Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick were unsuccessful in their bids for the 7th and 20th districts, respectively. 

Nathan's notes

Less than three months out from Election Day, control of Congress remains in play and Republicans continue to look vulnerable in both House and Senate battlegrounds, according to Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections. 

Inside Elections recently updated its race ratings in 11 midterm contests across the country, 10 of them in Democrats’ favor, Nathan writes. 

What we’re reading 

Primary colors: Democratic voters in Connecticut opted for generational change by casting out longtime Rep. John B. Larson last week. NOTUS traveled north on Interstate 91 and to see if the same dynamic is at play across the border in Massachusetts, where 77-year-old Rep. Richard E. Neal is facing an under-the-radar challenge from Jeromie Whalen, a 39-year-old public school teacher.

#MISEN: Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s primary win this month could complicate Democrats’ path to the Senate majority, The Washington Post reports, with many Jewish voters alarmed at his harsh criticism of Israel. 

Trickle-down campaigning: Democrats are looking to strong gubernatorial nominees in Pennsylvania and Iowa to help boost candidates running to flip key House seats, National Journal reports. 

No love lost here: NOTUS talked to Florida freshman Rep. Mike Haridopolos, who played a key role in recruiting Elijah to challenge Mills, believing the incumbent was a threat to the Republican House majority. 

Where is the tan suit?: WBEZ in Chicago is revisiting one of Washington’s most absurd political controversies as it issues a public call for information about former President Barack Obama’s infamous tan suit.

The Count: $1.8 million

That's how much former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema spent on security — between her official Senate account and her campaign committee — over the near-four-year period beginning in October 2021, when Vrindavan Gabbard Bellord, the younger sister of Tulsi Gabbard, joined her Senate staff. 

In the four years before the hire, Sinema's office and campaign security spending totaled just $1,175, federal filings show.

Notably, Gabbard Bellord was the one who employed Matthew J. Ammel, whose wife has sued the former senator under North Carolina's so-called homewrecker law for engaging in an extramarital affair with Ammel, as Sinema testified to in a July 31 deposition recently made public.

Gabbard Bellord left Sinema’s staff in October 2023, and Ammel went on to work for Sinema’s new security provider, Kinsaker Security Group, founded months earlier by another Senate office staffer, Shawn Kinsey. Between his Senate salary and campaign work for Sinema, who left office in 2025, Kinsey and his company were paid more than $1 million over the next two years. 

– By Roll Call’s Ryan Kelly

Key race: #NH01

Candidates: Both parties have a crowded field of candidates running to succeed Democrat Chris Pappas in New Hampshire’s 1st District. On the Democratic side, the field includes Stefany Shaheen, a former member of the Portsmouth City Council and the daughter of retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen; Marine Corps veteran Maura Sullivan, who previously ran for the seat in 2018; state Rep. Heath Howard; Hampton Select Board Chairwoman Carleigh Beriont; Army National Guardsman and former Pentagon lawyer Christian Urrutia; former state Rep. Bill Conlin; Sarah Chadzynski; Matthew Emerson; and Sarah Bella Spinosa. Republican contenders include businessman Anthony DiLorenzo; businesswoman Hollie Noveletsky, who lost the Republican primary for the seat two years ago; state Rep. Brian Cole; and Lindsey Anderson.

Why it matters: Pappas, who has held the battleground seat since 2019, is running for the state’s open Senate seat. On the Democratic side, Shaheen and Sullivan are locked in an increasingly tense race. Republicans, meanwhile, are hoping to flip the district, which once routinely swung between the parties but has been in Democratic hands for the past decade. 

Cash dash: Sullivan has led the fundraising race so far, bringing in $3.3 million through the end of June, with $1.6 million banked. Shaheen reported raising $2.2 million and had $1.2 million on hand. Urrutia raised just over $1 million, the only other Democrat to reach that threshold at the end of the second quarter, closing with $220,000 in the bank. On the GOP side, DiLorenzo raised $2.3 million through June 30, including a personal loan of under $1.7 million, and had $1.2 million banked. Noveletsky raised $551,000 and had $292,000 on hand, while Cole hauled in $483,000 and had $126,000 available. A few outside groups have been spending in the Democratic primary. Shaheen has benefited from spending from Article One PAC, LCV Victory Fund and No Kings PAC. VoteVets has spent over $1 million to support Sullivan, who has also benefited from outlays from the Servant-Leader Fund Inc.

Backers: Sullivan has touted her support from fellow veterans, including Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger and New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, as well as Reps. Pat Ryan, Jason Crow and Chrissy Houlahan, among others. Shaheen has touted endorsements from the American Federation of Teachers and the League of Conservation Voters Action Fund, as well as Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly. DiLorenzo won Trump’s coveted endorsement, and is also supported by the NRCC and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan. Melissa Bailey, who was previously running for the seat, has also been campaigning for him.

What they’re saying: Shaheen has made health care a central focus of her campaign, saying in a recent ad that Trump was “slashing your health care to pay for his ballrooms, bombs, and tax breaks for billionaires.” This week, she released another ad, accusing Sullivan of funding her campaign with mostly out-of-state donations. Sullivan, a member of the so-called Hell Cats, has emphasized her military service, campaigning this week with Sherrill. In one ad, she notes her service in Iraq and ties it to the current conflict with Iran: “I’ll be damned if I’m going to sit by while Trump gets us into another costly foreign war,” she says. Both Howard and Urrutia have sought to fill the progressive lane. DiLorenzo has touted his business acumen and appeared with Energy Secretary Chris Wright this week. Cole has touted his experience in the state House, while Noveletsky, in a recent debate, pointed to her family’s steel fabrication company, stressing the need for more domestic manufacturing jobs. 

Terrain: The 1st District covers much of the eastern part of New Hampshire, including Manchester, the state’s largest city. Kamala Harris carried the district by 2 points in 2024, while Pappas won a fourth term with 54 percent of the vote. Inside Elections rates the race Lean Democratic. 

Wild card: Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte, who is favored to win a second term this year, carried the 1st District by 10 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections.

South Carolina Republicans on Tuesday will pick their nominee to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham on the November ballot. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her brother’s remaining term, and Rep. Ralph Norman are facing off in a run-off election. Trump is scheduled to rally with Graham in Myrtle Beach on Friday. 

Other run-off elections taking place Tuesday include primaries for governor and Senate in Oklahoma and an all-Democratic race in Georgia to choose a successor to the late Rep. David Scott.

news.title: Democrats Want Us to Believe That Their ‘Big Tent’ Isn’t Just for Socialists
news.text:
The strategy is playing out in Texas, Alaska, Georgia, and Arizona, states where the GOP holds a strong registration edge or thin margins have decided recent races. In other words, states where a Democrat running there needs Republican-leaning voters to have a prayer of winning.

"Every Democrat says we need a bigger tent, but it's up to each candidate to show that they actually mean it," said Andrew Mamo, spokesperson for The Bench, a group backing center-left Democrats.

In Texas, Democrat Senate candidate James Talarico hired a little-known former staffer from Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) office as his deputy policy director. Did it really mean anything? No, but he gets the swooning media coverage, making him sound like a reasonable Democrat as a result.

"My message to Texans across the political spectrum is clear: no matter which party you belong to, which part of the state you're from, or which candidate you supported in the primary — you have a place in this campaign," Talarico said in a statement explaining the hire.

It’s an amusing strategy, but Talarico's chances run into a rather big problem that trivial campaign hires won’t fix: he's wildly out of step with the mainstream on transgender issues, and no amount of Cornyn alumni on his payroll changes that. This is the same guy who “loves trans kids” and says “God is nonbinary.” Trump won Texas by 14 points in 2024; if anyone thinks Talarico has a prayer, they’re deluding themselves.

Recommended: Scott Jennings Schools CNN Panel on Biden's Inflation Disaster

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), facing Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), rolled out endorsements this month from three Republicans, including former Sen. Jeff Flake (R-Ariz.). Calling Flake a real Republican is generous. He’s just another anti-Trumper who didn’t fit in the GOP and went on to endorse Biden in 2020. "Endorsements overall are overrated," Flake told NOTUS. "But cross-party endorsements can help and have helped in the past. I think it's a smart strategy."

In Arizona, Gov. Katie Hobbs (D-Ariz.) tapped John Giles, a Republican former Mesa mayor who endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024, as her running mate for lieutenant governor. Democrat strategist Steve Schale, who isn’t involved in that race, thinks it's a smart bet. "The one thing you hear in swing voter focus groups over and over again is exhaustion with politics," Schale said. "Her math problem is similar to [Talarico's], and it really doesn't lose her much."

"Hobbs is making a bet — that appears to be working — that voters are just over it and want grown a** adults to get things done," Schale added. "I love it — and I wish more Dems in lean red states running for governor would do it." Hobbs literally vetoes everything the GOP-controlled legislature does, but okay, go with that.

This is all happening in a party that is ready to boot Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) for only voting with his party 95% of the time, by the way.

Republican National Committee spokeswoman Natalie Baldassarre isn't buying the makeover. "Democrats trying to appeal to Republican voters is like a career criminal suddenly running for sheriff," she said. "All of these far-left extremists support open borders, higher taxes and endless government control. Democrats should get their own house in order before they come looking for new voters."

The ironic thing is that, in the end, no one is voting for one candidate over another based on a campaign hire or a meaningless endorsement. Democrats can hire all the Republican staffers they want, and dredge up washed up pseudo Republicans for endorsements all they want. They're still asking voters to believe they're something they've never been.

news.title: Democrats’ Southern Strategy
news.text:
Don’t believe the Democratic National Committee’s official storyline—the DNC’s decision to make South Carolina the first Democratic presidential primary in 2028 isn’t about introducing more racial diversity into the early contests. It’s actually about keeping power in the hands of the party establishment, the people who backed Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Joe Biden in 2020, and who are likely to wind up supporting Kamala Harris in 2028.

The fix is in.

South Carolina was the establishment’s firewall against Bernie Sanders’ left-wing insurgency twice over. In 2016, Sanders nearly beat Hillary Clinton in the first caucus, in Iowa, and went on to defeat her in the New Hampshire primary. Four years later, there was a brief moment when Sanders looked like the frontrunner—until he got clobbered by Joe Biden in South Carolina.

It’s true that the black voters who make South Carolina’s primaries more racially diverse than the contests in Iowa or New Hampshire are also less politically radical, so it’s easy for the DNC to say it’s not trying to choke off support for the socialist wing of the party, it’s just giving black voters more of a say.

The Democratic Socialists of America, the left fringe of the party, is disproportionately white—even its New York City chapter is 60 percent white, according to DSA’s own membership polling.

That’s astonishing considering NYC itself is only 34 percent white.

news.title: Focus groups: Deep anxiety about the economy drives undecided voters in two key Senate races
news.text: Concerns about the economy and high costs are driving the thinking of undecided voters in Iowa and Georgia, according to new focus group conversations, as two states that will be central to the fight for the Senate barrel toward Election Day. “Nothing has gotten better as far as the cost of living, inflation — food is astronomical, gas,” said Patty O., a 59-year-old Georgia Republican who voted for Donald Trump in 2024. “The cost of living is so high right now.” Patty was among a dozen voters up for grabs in two Senate races who participated this week in focus groups produced by Syracuse University and the research firms Engagious and Sago and observed by NBC News. The group comprised six independents, five Republicans and one Democrat. Nine voted for Trump for president two years ago, when he won both states, while three supported then-Vice President Kamala Harris. All but three of the voters said they feel more anxious about the economy today than when Trump returned to office. Eight said Trump is not focused enough on the issue. These voters’ anxieties reflect recent polling detailing broad concerns about the state of the economy — and Trump’s handling of it. Unlike a poll, which uses statistical methods to demonstrate how a larger population feels, focus groups dig deeper into how a handful of people feel about key questions facing the country. With less than three months until the midterm elections, these voters were still weighing whom to support in the Senate races, though some have picked favorites for governor. But the economy will loom large in their decisions. Asked whether the economy will be a major consideration in their votes in November, all but one said yes. “Among these undecided voters, pervasive economic anxiety is the animating issue in the midterms — not Iran, not immigration, not Israel/Gaza,” said Rich Thau of Engagious, who moderated the sessions. Economic anxiety Overall, eight of the 12 undecided voters said they disapproved of Trump’s job performance during his second term, even though a majority of the disapprovers voted for him in 2024. The most common criticisms focused on his stewardship of the economy. Jamie G., a 55-year-old Iowa independent who voted for Trump, said he is “disillusioned with pretty much everything he’s done since he took office.” “He was going to end conflicts on the first day, which he didn’t do. Instead, he’s gotten us into needless wars. His tariffs have caused prices — it’s been like a tax on things for the American people,” he said. “He’s more worried about his vanity projects, like the reflecting pool and his ballroom, than he is with the real problems in this country,” Jamie G. added. Those who broadly approved of Trump’s tenure pointed to his immigration policies or how they saw him as different from other politicians. Tyler R., a 24-year-old Iowa Republican who voted for Trump, said he approves of about 60% of what Trump has done in office, appreciating “more discipline regarding our country’s immigration policy,” as well as his attempt to “start negotiations with Russia, however successful those have been.” However, he added that he has also been “frustrated” by Trump, raising concerns about tariffs’ increasing prices and about the war in Iran. Others echoed those sentiments about the stock market’s performance, like Drew G., a 59-year-old Georgia Republican. “Financially speaking, I keep looking at my investments, my 401(k), and it keeps going up,” he said, adding that Trump is “not as much of a politician as some people are. He may say some things that get people frustrated, myself included, but he doesn’t really care what he says. He’s not trying to get anybody’s approval.” Others saw the stock market’s gains as a double-edged sword. “I have extensively made a lot of money in investments, so that’s the only positive. And the positive of that obviously didn’t outweigh the negative,” said Jennifer B., a 43-year-old Iowa independent who voted for Trump. “I’m making a ridiculous amount of money, that’s for sure, but I can’t spend that,” she said. “It is just in stocks ... and it’s for the future.” Later in the focus group, Jennifer B., like more than half the participants, said that Trump isn’t focused enough on improving the economy and that she was frustrated by his lack of delivery on his campaign promises to bring prices down. “It’s not like it’s unusual from a politician, but those are pretty big deals to promise and then not fulfill those promises,” she said. These voters’ economic anxiety spanned all facets of their lives. They detailed worries about the cost of healthcare, gas, food, utilities and everything in between. Some are forgoing major purchases, cutting back on things that bring them joy or doing things like selling a laptop to cover bills. Sarah M., a 47-year-old Iowa voter who backed Harris in 2024 and used to consider herself a Democrat before she became an independent, said middle-class Americans like her are “being killed” by the economy. “My taxes dang near bankrupted us last year; we didn’t see any benefit of that. Our groceries, I have to drive 45 minutes just to be able to afford my groceries, but then you’re dealing with the gas prices on top of that,” she said. Patty O., the Georgia Republican, said she stopped buying orange juice and gave up her membership at a boutique gym, “which I loved going to, but I couldn’t justify the cost anymore.” “Even my utilities have gone up tremendously since last summer, and I don’t know what’s next. What else can I do to lower the cost or make more money?” she asked. Few voters said the Iran war was top of mind, but some pointed to the drawn-out conflict as a reason they are frustrated with Trump or as something that is hurting their wallets. Drew G. of Georgia said the shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz is “getting us less supplies over here, less gas over here. So the prices are going up a lot. I see it every time I go to the grocery store.” Midterm choices A majority of these voters disapproved of Trump and almost all were anxious about the economy, and half of them said their views of him would factor into their votes in the midterm. “We heard real disappointment and frustration with President Trump for getting the U.S. into a war that’s made things more expensive and for perceptions he’s too distracted by vanity projects or political fights to focus on pocketbook issues,” said Margaret Talev, director of the Institute for Democracy, Journalism and Citizenship at Syracuse University, which hosts the focus group project. “Still, most of these voters simply weren’t thinking tactically about using their midterm ballots to keep the White House in check. So Democrats shouldn’t assume rising anti-Trump sentiment will carry them in House, Senate or governor’s races,” Talev added. But negative views of Trump and the economy could present an opening among some voters like Tyler R., the Iowa Republican who broadly approved of Trump’s presidency but did raise concern about prices. Tyler said he sees political polarization as “a big problem” and would be drawn to a candidate who wants to work across the aisle. “I can count on one hand the number of Democrats that I voted for,” Tyler said. “I would consider voting for someone in the Democratic Senate race probably more because of what I’ve observed from the first two years of Trump’s presidency than I would in the past.” But Tyler and most of the other Iowa panelists could not identify Democratic nominee Josh Turek, a state representative, when they were shown his picture, nor could they say much about him. A few identified Rep. Ashley Hinson, the Republican nominee, with one noting that she had been a local TV news anchor. One voter said he believed Hinson was more moderate than the average Republican. Four of the five Iowa panelists said they would support Democrats’ pick for governor, State Auditor Rob Sand. “He seems to be more middle of the road and more willing to work with Republicans,” said MacKenzie R., a 34-year-old Iowa Republican who voted for Trump. Like other voters in both panels, MacKenzie raised concerns about Democrats’ moving too far to the left, saying, “What makes me nervous about them are the ones who are more on the socialist side.” But she viewed Sand as a different kind of Democrat, saying he has a “bipartisan attitude.” MacKenzie also sharply criticized the GOP nominee for governor, businessman Zach Lahn. Echoing Democratic attacks, she said Lahn “spends a lot of time in Kansas and seems like he lives there more than he lives in Iowa.” The Georgia voters in the focus group still wanted to learn more about their two Senate candidates, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff and GOP Rep. Mike Collins, before they make their decisions. Most did not know much about Collins beyond his strong support for Trump. Three of them have already decided to support Republican Rick Jackson in the governor’s race, pointing to his rise from the foster care system to billionaire businessman, with one voter saying Jackson “pulled himself up by the bootstraps.” The others were undecided in the race between Jackson and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee. While most voters said the economy would be a major factor in their votes, a few named other issues, including the war in Iran and data centers, a burgeoning issue in this year’s elections. Ron S., a 43-year-old Georgia independent who voted for Trump, said he would support a candidate who favors “minimizing the infrastructure of data centers and also finding ways to prevent further harm to the environment,” raising concerns that they also cause electricity prices to spike and limit access to reliable power sources. Patty O., the Georgia Republican, said she had a more positive view, saying, “I do think that data centers bring jobs.” Still, the economy remained the most important issue for these voters, like Alice N., a 47-year-old Georgia Republican who backed Trump. “I’m leaning more towards voting for somebody that is going to do more for the economy — to bring the cost of living down, to bring gas prices down, make it cheaper to go to the grocery store and do all those kinds of things,” she said.

news.title: La Résistance Is Kaput, and So Are Dems. Long Live the DSA?
news.text:
Since then, Democrats have remained obsessed with Orange Man Bad as the entire agenda of their party. Its establishment heavily recruited La Résistance candidates in the midterm primary cycle, expecting their voters to rally to the TDS anthem.

It's kind of been a rough set of primaries for Heroes of the Resistance 1.0 between Vindman losing tonight, Dan Goldman losing his seat (although there were other issues there) and George Conway getting only 6% of the vote in NY-12. People want to move on.— Nate Silver (@NateSilver538) August 19, 2026

In retrospect, the strategy here is bizarre to the point of mental illness. One would think that Trump's popular-vote win in 2024 over the relentless Biden-Harris effort to make Trump's disqualification the issue of the election would have pushed party leadership to start developing a new argument for leadership. Instead, Democrats doubled down on TDS, especially figures like Gavin Newsom and Jon Ossoff, who thought TDS was a grand uniting message for the Left. 

Instead, it turned out to be a dead end. Again.

And what happens when a party keeps trying to win elections while offering nothing of substance? They leave themselves open to factions with a real agenda. That's especially true when radical factions promise real action while the establishment keeps offering the same old failed strategies. Axios takes note of the successes of Democratic Socialists in the vacuum left by the Democrat establishment and its failed promises:

Why it matters: In the first Trump administration, involvement in impeachment was a fast-track ticket to Democratic stardom. Now it's seen as little more than set-dressing for an unpopular party establishment."Being aggressive on accountability and corruption (such as with impeachment) is not enough," one House Democrat told Axios in a text message.Democratic primary voters, the Democrat said, "are looking for us to be more aggressive and bold on a whole host of issues. ... Standing up to Trump is a must, but it's not enough in 2026."Another House Democrat said of impeachment: "Members now realize that it's not that big of a deal. It's old hat ... Especially when you can't deliver."

This has been the risk all along. Democrats insisted they could stop Trump with impeachment, even though they were far short of votes in the Senate. They insisted they could stop Trump with lawfare and failed. They insisted they could stop Trump with a ginned-up and absurd 14th Amendment argument, and that also failed spectacularly. Now, in this midterm cycle, Democrats ran Trump impeachment figures in primaries promising that another impeachment would stop Trump.

Did they really think voters would fall for it again? Promising the moon and delivering a pebble is always a recipe for political failure. When the party offers nothing else but The End Of Trump This Time And We Really Mean It even after Trump won his biggest election result, no one can be surprised that voters don't want impeachment grifters around to remind them of that failure. 

Instead, voters in Democrat primaries chose the only other option available to them. David Frum at The Atlantic points out the same risk that DSA candidates present in this midterm cycle, and why Democrats may go from the Trump skillet into a Marxist flame-out:

The far left of the Democratic Party has never been as energized as the party’s center about Trump and democracy. A 2017 analysis in The Washington Post suggested that between 6 and 12 percent of people who voted for Bernie Sanders in the 2016 Democratic primaries voted for Trump in the general election. With many careful caveats, the analysis observed that these voters exceeded Trump’s margin of victory.In 2024, likewise, some leaders of the activist left noisily defected from the Harris-Walz ticket. For many of them, opposing Israel’s war against Hamas in Gaza mattered more than stopping a Trump presidency at home. The effect of this mobilization on the left is hard to measure, but The Nation was quick to insist that the Biden administration’s Gaza policy likely cost the party Michigan, because many Arabs and Muslims swung toward Trump. The article did not seriously consider whether culture politics, such as Kamala Harris’s support for transgender rights, influenced socially conservative Arab and Muslim voters, even though the city of Dearborn has long been a locus of anti-gay grassroots politics in the state. The claim that Harris lost to Trump because of Gaza may well be activist self-medication, but this kind of story about the election is telling.This year, the dulling of anti-Trump impetus on the left is even more visible and consequential. Again and again, primary voters have made choices that subordinate general-election concerns to factional power-seeking. Democratic leaders—the dreaded “Establishment”—have promoted highly plausible candidates for statewide office in North Carolina, Texas, and other suddenly competitive states. But the insurgent left has again and again upset leadership plans with high-risk choices to serve its own factional agenda, putting at risk once-probable Senate victories in Maine, Michigan, and some House seats too.

And this also has a large contradiction at its core:

Many of the far-left candidates are aggressively obnoxious from a centrist’s point of view. Centrist Democrats are not socialists, not revolutionaries, and not disposed to blame Zionist conspiracies for every trouble in American life, including police brutality and urban gentrification. Why on earth would centrist Democrats in Michigan vote for a radical leftist who calls most Democrats hypocrites when the other choice on the ballot is a Republican campaigning on reducing housing costs by simplifying the government-approval process?

That's the big question in Michigan, but also in Maine, Texas, Florida, and maybe in Georgia too. The DSA's entire agenda consists of promises that cannot possibly be redeemed, platformed on a political/economic system that has only ever delivered shortages, tyranny, and misery. A handful of DSA radicals will enter Congress in January, thanks to early poaching in deep-blue districts, but they may not last long. At some point, the party will finally stop obsessing over Trump and start focusing on its survival.

At the moment, though, the Democrat Party is intellectually kaput. Unless and until they come up with a realistic alternative to the DSA that focuses on real deliverables, they'd better be prepared to lose a lot of elections under the red banners of the Marxists they allowed into their "big tent."
