news.title: Apple, Google News ‘favor Democrats’. Never endorsed a Republican presidential candidate. New study reveals
news.text: A new analysis by the conservative Media Research Center (MRC) claims that some of the most heavily promoted news outlets on Apple News and Google News have overwhelmingly backed Democratic presidential candidates in their editorial endorsements over the past four decades.The study argues that the pattern raises questions about the political diversity of news sources promoted by major digital news aggregators.MRC: Top-promoted outlets backed Democrats in every electionAccording to the MRC analysis, the five most-promoted outlets on Apple News and Google News that have a history of presidential endorsements collectively gave 31 endorsements to Democratic candidates and none to Republicans across the 10 presidential elections from 1988 through 2024.For Apple News, MRC identified 28 Democratic endorsements and zero Republican endorsements. USA Today was counted separately because it broke from its traditional non-endorsement policy in 2016 to issue an editorial warning against Donald Trump rather than endorse a Democratic candidate.For Google News, the outlets recorded 27 Democratic endorsements and zero Republican endorsements, with USA Today again issuing an anti-Trump editorial rather than a formal Democratic endorsement.The MRC describes the findings as evidence of a political imbalance among the news organizations most prominently featured by the platforms.Which outlets did MRC examine?For Apple News, the five most-promoted outlets with presidential endorsement histories were identified as:The Washington PostThe New York Times, including The AthleticThe GuardianUSA TodayThe Los Angeles TimesFor Google News, MRC identified:The New York TimesThe GuardianThe Washington PostUSA TodayThe AtlanticThe organizations have endorsed Democratic candidates in every presidential election covered by the study, according to MRC.Those endorsements included Michael Dukakis in 1988, Bill Clinton in 1992 and 1996, Al Gore in 2000, John Kerry in 2004, Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, Hillary Clinton in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Kamala Harris in 2024.MRC points to sharply worded Trump endorsementsThe report also examined the language used by several publications when endorsing candidates.MRC highlighted USA Today's 2016 editorial opposing Trump, in which the newspaper said he lacked the “temperament, knowledge, steadiness and honesty” required of a president.The New York Times' 2024 endorsement of Kamala Harris similarly praised her as a “dedicated public servant” with “care” and “competence,” while describing Trump as “morally unfit” and “temperamentally unfit.”The Washington Post's 2020 endorsement backed Biden as “exceptionally well-qualified” and “deeply empathetic,” while describing Trump as “the worst president of modern times,” according to the MRC report.The MRC argues that such language illustrates what it sees as a recurring contrast between favourable descriptions of Democratic candidates and highly critical portrayals of Republicans.Long-term pattern highlightedThe analysis goes back to 1988, when The New York Times described Democratic nominee Michael Dukakis as a “disciplined and serious man” with “decent instincts.”In 1992, The Washington Post called Bill Clinton the “only candidate” capable of reenergising the country and said then-President George H.W. Bush had “failed” the test of the presidency.The Post endorsed Clinton again in 1996, despite describing his administration as “disappointing” and “deficient.”The analysis says the pattern continued through the 2000s, with publications praising Barack Obama's intelligence and judgment while sharply criticising Republican candidates John McCain and Mitt Romney.MSN also shows a Democratic tilt, MRC saysThe MRC analysis also examined Microsoft's MSN, another major news aggregation platform.Among the five most-promoted MSN outlets with presidential endorsement histories were USA Today, The Washington Post, the Los Angeles Times, Rolling Stone and the San Francisco Chronicle.MRC found that these outlets issued 27 presidential endorsements since 1988, of which 25 went to Democrats and two to Republicans.Both Republican endorsements came from the San Francisco Chronicle and were for George H.W. Bush, in 1988 and 1992.Since then, according to MRC, the newspaper has endorsed Democratic candidates in every presidential election.What the MRC methodology looked atThe analysis used the MRC's Digital News Tracker to examine the top 20 stories promoted by Google News and MSN during specified periods between November 2025 and July 2026.Researchers also examined the top 20 stories promoted by Apple News from November 2025 through July 2026.They then identified the most-promoted outlets that had editorial boards with presidential endorsement histories and researched their endorsements over the 10 elections from 1988 through 2024.The MRC said it used historical newspaper databases, the Wayback Machine, Newspapers.com and other open-source databases to establish the endorsement records.What the findings do—and do not—showThe study documents the presidential endorsement histories of outlets promoted by the three aggregators. It does not, by itself, establish that Apple News, Google News or MSN intentionally promote those outlets because of their political positions.Likewise, a newspaper's presidential endorsement does not necessarily mean that every news story it publishes reflects the editorial board's political views.Still, the MRC argues that the concentration of outlets with Democratic endorsement histories is significant because news aggregators can influence which stories and publishers receive visibility among millions of users.

news.title: Jon Ossoff vs. Pete Buttigieg's Chances of Defeating JD Vance in 2028
news.text: A new Emerson College poll revealed which Democrats have the strongest lead over Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a 2028 presidential election matchup. The presidential field could soon start to take shape. Candidates typically begin announcing their runs after the midterms, though it’s not unprecedented for candidates to jump in even before those elections. Prospective candidates are already testing their messages and heading to key primary states to build their name recognition and make inroads with voters. Although the first votes won’t be cast for more than a year, polls can signal which candidates have early momentum among the electorate. Donors and voters can use these early signals to gauge a candidate’s viability, and the numbers matter to a candidate's ability to fundraise and garner media attention. They generally measure initial name recognition of potential candidates and are subject to change once the primary season kicks off. The Democratic field is expected to be competitive and crowded, with individuals like former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg being named as potential candidates. On the Republican side, Vance and Rubio are viewed as leading contenders if they choose to run. Which Democrats Perform Best Against Vance and Rubio? The new poll tested potential matchups of the 2028 general election. It surveyed 1,000 likely voters from August 16-17, 2026, and had a margin of error of ±3 percentage points. Buttigieg held 5-point leads against both Vance and Rubio, leading each Republican 49 percent to 44 percent, according to the poll. Ossoff led Vance by 5 points as well, 49 percent to 44 percent, while he led Rubio by 3 points, 47 percent to 44 percent. Newsom led Vance by 5 points, 49 percent to 44 percent and Rubio by 2 points, 48 percent to 46 percent, according to the poll. Harris led Vance by 4 points, 49 percent to 45 percent. However, Rubio held a 5-point lead against Harris, 48 percent to 43 percent. Meanwhile, both Republicans held a lead over Ocasio-Cortez, a favorite among progressives ahead of the primary. Vance led Ocasio-Cortez by 2 points, 46 percent to 44 percent, while Rubio held a 5-point lead, 48 percent to 43 percent. Newsweek reached out to representatives for Buttigieg, Harris, Newsom, Ocasio-Cortez, Ossoff, Rubio and Vance for comment via email. Who Is Leading Democratic Primary in the Polls? The latest polls of the Democratic primary suggest the field remains splintered, though Harris, who is well-known across the electorate, has maintained a lead in recent surveys. An Echelon Insights poll recently found Harris leading with 18 percent, followed by Buttigieg (13 percent), Newsom (12 percent), Ocasio-Cortez (11 percent), Arizona Senator Mark Kelly (7 percent), Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro (6 percent) and Ossoff (5 percent). Several other candidates received less than 5 percent in the poll. It surveyed 1,002 likely voters from August 13 to 17, 2026 and had a margin of error of ±3.4 percentage points. A recent Emerson College poll found Buttigieg leading with 19 percent, followed by Newsom (17 percent), Ossoff (13 percent), Ocasio-Cortez (13 percent), Harris (8 percent), Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear (7 percent), and Shapiro (5 percent), with other candidates polling in the lower single digits. It polled 1,110 likely voters from July 19 to 20, 2026, and had a margin of error of ±2.9 percentage points. Who Is Leading the Republican Primary in the Polls? On the Republican side, a handful of potential candidates have been leading recent polling, though several others could also end up running. The Echelon poll found Vance up with 39 percent, followed by Rubio (22 percent), Florida Governor Ron DeSantis (10 percent) and Donald Trump, Jr. (8 percent). The Emerson College poll found Vance leading with 39 percent, closely followed by Rubio at 38 percent. DeSantis received 5 percent support in that poll. What Have Potential Candidates Said About Running? Vance In June, Vance told CBS News he would discuss plans to run in 2028 after the midterms. "I have no doubt that the president of the United States is going to be very supportive of anything that I ultimately decide to do," Vance told the news station. "But we really just haven't talked about what that thing will be." Harris Harris, who has traveled to states like Michigan and South Carolina in recent months, has suggested she could run again. “I might. I am thinking about it,” she told the Reverend Al Sharpton in April after he asked during the National Action Network’s annual convention if she planned to run for president in 2028. Harris noted that she “served for four years being a heartbeat away from the presidency of the United States.” “I spent countless hours in my West Wing office footsteps away from the Oval Office," she said. "I spent countless hours in the Oval Office and the Situation Room. I know what the job is, and I know what it requires.” Newsom Newsom discussed the possibility of running in a June 2025 interview with The Wall Street Journal. “I'm not thinking about running, but it's a path that I could see unfold,” he said. Newsom also told reporters in July that whether he joins the race would be determined by “fate.” “I really believe it’s fate,” he said. “You meet the moment, you represent something where you can uniquely and distinctively make the case that your voice matters in a competitive field where there will be stadiums full of Democrats. Every conceivable stripe of Democrat will be on display.” Ocasio-Cortez Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, a former adviser to President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." Ossoff Ossoff has said he does not plan to run. “I have zero interest in running for president in 2028, and frankly zero interest in the 2028 fantasy football right now,” he said on MS Now. What's Next? While there is no immediate deadline for a prospective 2028 presidential candidate to enter the race, political observers are likely to focus first on the outcome of the 2026 midterm elections on November 3. The results are expected to provide an early indication of the issues, voter coalitions and political figures that could shape the next presidential contest. Following the midterms, potential White House hopefuls are expected to ramp up fundraising, travel to early-voting states and build campaign organizations ahead of what could become a crowded 2028 field. Primary calendars and candidate filing deadlines are not yet finalized, but the race is expected to accelerate significantly once the 2026 elections conclude. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas

news.title: Philly named one of three finalists to host 2028 Democratic National Convention
news.text:
Officials have narrowed the search for a host city for the 2028 Democratic National Convention, and Philadelphia is one of three still in the running. 

The city was named as a finalist Thursday morning by the Democratic National Committee alongside Denver and Boston. Chicago, the host of the 2024 DNC, and Atlanta are no longer being considered, although officials did not say why. 

The political event, held every four years, is traditionally where a political party formally announces its presidential and vice presidential candidates for the upcoming election. The 2028 DNC will be held Aug. 7-10. The Republican National Convention will be held in Houston, although official dates have not yet been announced. 

According to the Associated Press, officials visited all five cities in the spring to look at logistical metrics and fundraising capacity, among other considerations. The three finalist cities emerged with "incredibly strong bids," Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin told the outlet. A final decision is expected later this year. 

The strategy behind hosting the event in a swing state like Pennsylvania is that it could help drum up support from local voters and provide campaign infrastructure in an area that could tip the balance of an election. While Democratic candidates won the past three presidential elections in Colorado and Massachusetts, Republican Donald Trump won Pennsylvania in 2016 and 2024. 

In 2015, Philadelphia beat out Brooklyn, New York, and Columbus, Ohio, when it was announced as the 2016 DNC host city. The event drew thousands to the city, including celebrities Katy Perry, Sheila E., Carole King, Danny Glover, Rosario Dawson, Susan Sarandon, Paul Simon, Shailene Woodley, Stephen Colbert, Demi Lovato, Chloe Grace Moretz, Eva Longoria, Bernard Hopkins, Debra Messing and Jenkintown native Bradley Cooper. 

There was also a number of protests were held in the city criticizing the political gathering. It also brought fiberglass donkey statues, which were placed on sidewalks in a number of neighborhoods, and a huge surge in the use of dating apps Tinder and Grindr. 

Denver last hosted the event in 2008, and Boston did so in 2004. 

With the election more than two years away, it's currently unclear who will be on the Democratic ticket. However, U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.), Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.), former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are being floated as possible contenders.
news.summary: Philadelphia on Thursday was named one of three finalists to host the 2028 Democratic National Convention. Denver and Boston are also still in the running. The last time Philadelphia hosted the event was 2016.

news.title: JD Vance Faces Major Warning Sign as New Poll Shows Democrat Crushing Him
news.text:
Jon Ossoff is emerging as one of the strongest-performing Democrats in a hypothetical 2028 presidential matchup against JD Vance, despite the Georgia senator repeatedly saying he has “zero interest” in a White House bid.

A new Emerson College Polling survey of 1,000 likely voters nationwide shows Ossoff leading Vance by five points, 49 percent to 44 percent.

That advantage tightens when the Republican named in the matchup is Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with Ossoff’s lead shrinking to three points.

The results place Ossoff among the top tier of Democratic figures tested by Emerson in early 2028 election polling, though the survey reflects a set of hypothetical contests rather than a firm forecast of the next presidential race.

Still, there is another reason the Georgia Democrat’s numbers are drawing fresh scrutiny.

Ossoff recently ignited a political backlash after taking aim at Trump with a sharp remark about aide Natalie Harp, saying the president would rather “build his ballroom and travel with Natalie” than do his job.

The comment rapidly spread online, becoming a viral political moment that pushed Ossoff deeper into the 2028 presidential conversation and underscored his willingness to confront Trump directly.

For now, however, the 39-year-old Georgia senator is focused on his Senate re-election campaign, not a run for the White House.

He has repeatedly rejected speculation about a presidential campaign, saying in June that he was ‘not running for president in 2028’ and had ‘no interest’ in doing so.

For now, Ossoff’s stated focus is Georgia.

But a big re-election victory in the Peach State could change the political conversation.

A decisive win would give Ossoff another statewide victory, greater national visibility and a fresh mandate heading into the period when Democrats will begin seriously considering their 2028 options.

The Emerson survey tested Vance and Rubio against five Democrats: Ossoff, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, California Governor Gavin Newsom, New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The August poll has a margin of error of +/- 3 percent. 

A national vote does not elect the president. The White House is won through the Electoral College — meaning the battleground states, not a nationwide popularity contest, will ultimately decide who takes the Oval Office next. 

Buttigieg produced the same five-point advantage against both Republican contenders, making him the only Democrat in the survey to hold an identical margin against Vance and Rubio.

Buttigieg leads Vance by five points, 49 percent to 44 percent, the same lead Ossoff had secured. Ossoff’s advantage was three against Rubio.

Newsom also led Vance, with his advantage narrowing to two points against Rubio.

Harris led Vance by four points but trailed Rubio by five, illustrating how much the Republican matchup mattered in the hypothetical contests.

The presidential hypotheticals come amid a difficult national environment for Republicans in the survey.

President Donald Trump’s job approval stands at 40 percent, compared with 56 percent who disapprove. Among independents, disapproval reaches 66 percent, while 92 percent of Democrats disapprove.

The economy is the top issue for voters at 37 percent, followed by threats to democracy and healthcare, both at 16 percent, and immigration at 13 percent.

And the survey contains another striking finding: 23 percent of likely voters say they consider themselves supporters of the Democratic Socialists of America, while 60 percent say they are not supporters and 17 percent are unsure. Among Democrats, 46 percent identify as DSA supporters.

The Democratic Socialists’ growing push inside the Democratic Party has produced a string of headline-grabbing primary battles this summer — with mixed results.

In Wisconsin, Democratic socialist Francesca Hong led the governor’s race in the polls before narrowly losing the August 11 primary to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley by roughly 3,000 votes.

But elsewhere, the movement has scored major victories. Michigan progressive Abdul El-Sayed won his Senate primary.

Florida state Representative Angie Nixon, a DSA-backed Democratic socialist, stunned the political establishment by defeating heavily funded rival Alex Vindman to win the Democratic Senate nomination.

news.title: NABJ’s Errin Haines’ Bold Defense of Accountability in Black Media
news.text:
After sports commentator Stephen A. Smith received the Thumbs Down Award at the National Association of Black Journalists convention last week, debates erupted over why the organization would “target” a Black man or accuse him of disparaging Black women like Michelle Obama and Kamala Harris.

Now, NABJ President Errin Haines is setting the record straight on why Smith will remain in the hot seat until accountability becomes evident.

Haines appeared on Roland Martin’s show to defend the decision, which she said was not “made casually.”

“I think we have to agree that there’s a clear through line,” she told Martin about this year’s honorees. “We’re looking at the forces that make it harder for Black journalists to do their jobs and harder for Black communities to be covered fairly and fully.”

The award itself has a history of confrontation. DeWayne Wickham, an NABJ co-founder and former president, created the Thumbs Down Award and previously used it to call out disgraced journalist Jayson Blair in 2003. The tradition reflected an idea that NABJ could celebrate Black journalists while challenging them when they fall short.

RELATED: Stephen A. Smith Reacts to Ryan Clark’s ESPN Exit, Proves Even the Network’s Biggest Star Has Limited Power

That history fueled Haines’ decision.

“It is really in the spirit of our old and visionary founders and past presidents that I felt that it was important to talk about this now,” Haines said.

We previously told you that NABJ recognized five people and institutions representing what she described as forces making it harder for Black communities to receive fair coverage – including government pressure, media decisions affecting diversity, treatment of Black journalists and influential commentators whose rhetoric can reinforce damaging stereotypes.

In addition to Smith, the Thumbs Down Award was given to CBS News, The Washington Post, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, and media executive DuJuan McCoy – all of whom faced criticism from NABJ and advocates over actions or decisions they say undermined Black journalists, diversity and fair coverage.

“Black America is under attack,” Wickham said during an interview with Haines and Martin. “We have to struggle to make sure that we can hold off these forces – these enemies – at our gate.”

He continued, “We need to understand that we cannot defeat the enemies at the gates if we do not take on and defeat the enemies within.”

For the organization’s current president, the award is about accountability and what happens when influential Black voices use their platforms in negative ways. “That means defending Black journalists when they are targeted,” Haines added, “but it also means challenging institutions or individuals when necessary.”

Smith clearly felt challenged. After receiving the award, he said that although he would “always strive to do better,” that did not negate what he called “the bullsh*t that the NABJ did.”

Afterward, Smith’s representatives invited Haines onto his show for a public conversation. She declined and instead offered a private conversation.

“I don’t believe that the first step would be, for me as president of NABJ, to go on to his program,” she told Martin. 

Haines also acknowledged Smith’s long relationship with NABJ and said she understood why the award landed differently for him. But that relationship, she argued, is precisely why the organization should be able to confront him.

“We think that he can do better,” she said. “That’s part of what community is supposed to be.”

For Haines, the award was not about canceling Stephen A. Smith. It was about reminding one of Black media’s most powerful personalities that influence comes with responsibility — and that accountability is part of community, too.
news.summary:
NABJ President Errin Haines explains why Stephen A. Smith received the Thumbs Down award, and why accountability remains central to Black journalism.

news.title: The man behind many of Trump's biggest legislative wins is leaving the White House
news.text:
President Donald Trump's longest-serving director of legislative affairs is departing this White House in the coming weeks, wrapping up nearly 600 wild, white-knuckle days of managing relations between the the 47th president and the Congress.

While Trump's massive 2024 electoral victory created powerful momentum in the early days of the administration, hard battles were quick to follow. The White House relied on knife's-edge majorities in both chambers, as well as a number of senior senators in particular who carried no love for the president — and no sure loyalty to his priorities.

'James has played a critical role in our many accomplishments with Congress.'

Just a week after Trump trounced Democratic nominee and Vice President Kamala Harris by 2,284,967 votes and 86 electoral points, former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) gave a speech to the neoconservative think tank AEI in which he promised to devote his remaining days in office to frustrating the incoming Republican administration.

While less strident than their leader, Sens. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), Susan Collins (R-Maine), and Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) promised similarly tough approaches. Both Collins and Murkowski backed former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley for president, though her campaign only ever won Washington, D.C., and all three of them had voted to impeach at the end of Trump's first term.

Despite formidable obstacles from the entire Democrat coalition and parts of the Grand Old Party itself, James Braid and his team were able to accomplish sweeping legislation on taxes, energy, the border, and spending in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act; send $70 billion to immigration and border enforcement with the Secure America Act, even after the ICE-involved Minneapolis shootings scattered Senate support; create a regulatory framework for stablecoin cryptocurrency with the Genius Act; claw back $9 billion in overspending with a Rescissions Act; and crack down on deadly fentanyl trafficking and revenge porn with the Halt and Take It Down acts.

Even while the president, the Congress, and the parties all duked it out, the legislative affairs team was able to notch a number of major bipartisan victories. Early on, the Laken Riley Act won Democrat votes to create new tools for states to detain criminal illegal aliens and, possibly more importantly, give states legal remedies when the federal government refused its responsibility to protect states being swamped by illegal immigration, as many experienced during the Biden administration.

Braid and his team were also instrumental in helping to form coalitions and grease tracks for the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. The bill was perhaps Washington's most populist reform of the past two years, working to lower housing prices and protect American families by taking on powerful, entrenched private equity interests that had been busily buying up entry-level homes in fast-growing markets, paying cash, and converting starter neighborhoods into permanent rental communities. While the vote ended up passing nearly unanimously, it was a battle to see it out of committees run by corporate-friendly Republicans and others unwilling to work with liberal Democrats.

Aside from legislative victories, Braid and his team successfully shepherded a number of deeply contentious nomination fights through an often hostile Senate, winning votes for Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Chairman of the Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh, and Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Blanche's confirmation was successful even after Trump targeted two of the Republican senators on the committee in their primary campaigns. While former Rep. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.) and Rep. Elise Stefanik (R-N.Y.) withdrew their nominations, this administration has never lost a confirmation vote.

"James has played a critical role in our many accomplishments with Congress, including the ONE BIG BEAUTIFUL BILL, beating the Democrats in two shutdown showdowns, passing the GENIUS Act, defeating a record number of War Powers resolutions, and in the confirmation of my Cabinet at the fastest rate in decades," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post Thursday morning.

Braid has long worked on Capitol Hill and joined the campaign as the legislative director for JD Vance, then a fast-moving and combative freshman senator. "James Braid had one of the toughest jobs in the entire Administration as White House Legislative Director and delivered for President Trump at every turn," Vance wrote Thursday morning. "He played a critical role in all of the administration’s achievements in Congress: largest tax cut ever, resources to carry out President Trump's historic immigration agenda and finish the border wall, defeating two Democratic shutdowns, a landmark first crypto bill, the fastest confirmation of the cabinet in decades and much more."

"I am profoundly grateful to President Trump and Vice President Vance for the opportunity to be a part of this extraordinary team and to serve in an administration that has worked with the Congress to deliver the largest tax relief in American history, the resources necessary to secure the border and build the wall across two reconciliation bills, the fastest confirmation of the Cabinet in 20 years, and defeating two Democratic shutdowns," said Braid in a statement.

news.title: Democrats’ Chances of Flipping the Senate 75 Days to Midterms—Polls
news.text: Democrats and Republicans are locked in a close race for control of the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, with recent polls showing single-digit races in several key contests that both parties are hoping to win in November. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in the midterms, so Democrats have been optimistic about their chances of winning a majority in the House of Representatives. But the Senate map is more difficult for Democrats. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, and Democrats have few clear targets and need to win seats in states that Trump won by double digits in 2024 to flip the Senate. Recent polls suggest the races in some of those more conservative states are going to be competitive in November, 75 days out from the November 3, 2026 midterms. What to Know Could the Senate Flip in 2026? What the Polls Show Democrats’ path to a Senate majority requires them to hold onto every seat they currently hold, flip the two seats they consider top targets, and then win two races in double-digit Trump states. The most competitive races in seats Democrats currently hold are in Georgia and Michigan, both of which narrowly backed Trump in the 2024 presidential election but did back former President Joe Biden in 2020. Democrats view GOP-held seats in Maine, which backed former Vice President Kamala Harris by 7 points, and North Carolina, which backed Trump by 3 points, as their top flip opportunities. Democrats hope that Trump’s declining national approval rating can expand the battleground and give them a chance at flipping more conservative states. Their top targets are Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, and polls show tight races for those seats. Shawn Donahue, a political science professor at the University at Buffalo, told Newsweek Democrats “absolutely” have a chance at winning control of the Senate in November. “If we would have had this discussion a year ago, the answer probably would have been not very likely,” he said. “I still think it’s a hard road for them to win control of the Senate, but it definitely seems like it’s doable now.” Overall, the national economy and issues such as gas prices and the cost of living are going to affect all of the races, but certain Trump administration policies could have different effects on different races. For instance, tariffs could be more impactful in states such as Maine, where Canadian tourism has dropped, and Iowa, a state with a large number of farmers. Democrats have been able to make tough races competitive by running strong candidates, he said. Stephen Farnsworth, political science professor at the University of Mary Washington, told Newsweek the odds of Democrats flipping the Senate are “about 50/50.” “The good news for Republicans is that the path to keeping their majority runs through states that President Trump won two years ago; the bad news is that polls show that Democratic voters are far more motivated than Republicans and that President Trump is particularly unpopular at the moment,” he said. The economy will be critical, he said. “President Trump promised to make things better, and most voters say he has made things worse. The price of gasoline is back up, and food and housing costs are increasing. Voters blame Trump's decision to start a war in Iran for part of the reason prices are continuing to increase,” he said. Bernadette Breslin, National Republican Senatorial Committee press secretary, told Newsweek, “Chuck Schumer continues to surrender his party to tax-and-spend socialists like Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, and Angie Nixon who will cost Democrats their chances at a Senate majority this November.” Newsweek reached out to the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for comment via email. Here is a look at where polling stands in each key race: Alaska Alaska backed Trump by 13 points in 2024, and it is traditionally viewed as a more conservative state with an independent streak. But the pro-Democratic national environment and candidacy of former Representative Mary Peltola, the only Democrat to represent it statewide in recent years, has given Democrats optimism about their chances of flipping the seat. Peltola is probably “the only Democrat that could have put the seat in play,” according to Donahue. Alaska uses a ranked-choice system and nonpartisan primary, so four candidates will be on the ballot in November. Peltola and GOP Senator Dan Sullivan received the most votes in this week’s primary; the other two general election spots had not been called by the Associated Press by Thursday morning. The latest poll from Alaska Survey Research showed Peltola with a 2-point lead over Sullivan, 51 percent to 49 percent. It surveyed 1,371 likely voters from August 2 to 5, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Data for Progress poll, which surveyed 578 likely voters from July 28 to August 4, showed Peltola up 6 points, 53 percent to 47 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. However, a poll from The New York Times and Siena University, conducted among 593 likely voters from June 15 to 29, showed Sullivan up 2 points, 47 percent to 45 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. Notably, Alaska is a vast, rural state that can be difficult at times to poll. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as a toss-up. Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who first entered office in 2021, has built up a polling lead in the Peach State. Although Georgia backed Trump in 2016 and 2024, it gave its electoral votes to Biden in 2020. Ossoff has proven to be popular in the state and has even been floated as a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate. A new poll from InsiderAdvantage released this week found 50 percent of Georgia voters surveyed said they would back Ossoff in November, while 43 percent said they plan to vote for Collins, a sitting representative from Georgia's 10th District. Seven percent of respondents said they were undecided about how they would vote in the general election. The poll surveyed 800 likely voters from August 16 to August 17 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.46 percentage points. It was first reported by James Magazine, a statewide political publication in Georgia. A poll from AARP found Ossoff up 9 points over Collins, 52 percent to 43 percent. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research among 1,060 likely voters from July 13 to July 16, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A recent Wick survey showed Ossoff up 4 points with 46.7 percent to Collins’ 42.9 percent. It surveyed 1,175 likely voters from June 27 to June 30, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. A poll for Fox News put Ossoff's support at 56 percent compared to Collins’ 43 percent—a whopping 13-point margin. It was conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research among 1,002 registered voters from June 23 to June 27. The Cook Political Report rates the race as Lean Democratic. Iowa Iowa was once a premier battleground, having backed former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012, but it has shifted rightward, backing Trump in each of his three runs, including by 13 points in 2024. But Democrats view it as competitive in this year's midterms. Republican Senator Joni Ernst is retiring, and Republican Representative Ashley Hinson and Democratic state legislator Josh Turek are running to replace her. The latest polls show a close race despite the state’s conservative lean. An Emerson College poll showed Hinson with a slight lead over Turek, 47.5 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 712 likely voters from August 2-4, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.7 percentage points. A poll from The New York Times and Siena University showed Hinson with a 2-point lead, 48 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 600 likely voters from June 15 to 27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. However, a Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, showed Turek up 4 points, 50 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,003 registered voters from June 23 to 27, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. The Cook Political Report views the race as Lean Republican. Donahue said Turek is a candidate who may be able to win over independents and moderate Republicans, but that Hinson is also a “good candidate” for Republicans. Tariffs are likely to be a key issue in the state, he said. “The tariffs and diesel fuel prices are really hitting Iowa,” he said. “Iowa is a very agriculture dependent state, and a lot of the farmers have lost some of their markets.” Maine In Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins is running against Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president who became the nominee after progressive political newcomer Graham Platner withdrew from the race. Maine generally leans toward Democrats, but Collins has been able to win in tough environments in the past because of her personal popularity and moderate credentials in the state. The Senate race in Maine was also upended in recent weeks. Platner’s exit from the race came after he faced sexual assault allegations, which he has denied. A series of polls showed a tightening race against Collins, and Democrats were increasingly concerned that he would be unable to win in November. His exit gave Democrats some relief, as they believed a candidate without scandals would stand a better chance of defeating Collins. Democrats replaced him on the ballot with Jackson, another progressive who unsuccessfully ran for governor. There is a “reason Collins has been able to win a Democratic-leaning state” in the past, but she is facing the toughest environment she’s ever run in, Donahue said. The latest polls of the race give Jackson a modest lead, though Republicans note that polls have been off in Maine in the past. A Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research, showed Jackson up 2 points, 48 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,000 registered voters from August 6 to 10, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Hart Research Associates poll, sponsored by the Democratic-aligned Senate Majority PAC, showed Jackson up 4 points, 49 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 802 likely voters from July 27 to August 1, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percentage points. Meanwhile, a University of New Hampshire poll showed Jackson with a 3-point lead, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,178 likely voters from July 15 to 20, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. The race is viewed as a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. Michigan Michigan is one of the most evenly divided battlegrounds, backing Trump by less than 2 points in 2024 after narrowly backing Biden in 2020. With Peters retiring, progressive public health official Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens to win the Democratic nomination to replace him in a contentious primary, while former Representative Mike Rogers won the Republican nomination. Polls suggest Michigan could be one of the closest races of the midterms. A Susquehanna Polling and Research survey, conducted among 800 likely voters from August 11 to 17, 2026, showed El-Sayed up 7 points, 46 percent to 39 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.46 percentage points. A Fox News poll, conducted among 1,006 registered voters from August 6 to 10, showed Rogers up 4 points, 51 percent to 47 percent. The poll’s margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points. The race is considered a toss-up by the Cook Political Report. New Hampshire In New Hampshire, Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is retiring, leaving open a seat in a state Harris won by about 3 points in 2024. The primary hasn’t been held yet, but Representative Chris Pappas is viewed as the Democratic frontrunner, while former Senator John Sununu and former Massachusetts Senator Scott Brown are running on the Republican side. A St. Anselm College poll showed Pappas up 12 points over Brown, 48 percent to 36 percent, and 6 points over Sununu, 47 percent to 41 percent. It surveyed 1,614 registered voters from June 24 to 25, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.4 percentage points. Meanwhile, a UNH poll showed Pappas up 14 points over Brown, 52 percent to 38 percent, and 3 points over Sununu, 47 percent to 44 percent. It surveyed 2,232 likely voters from June 18 to 23, 2026. The Cook Political Report views the race as Lean Democratic. North Carolina Democrats have not won a Senate race in North Carolina since 2008 but believe 2026 could be the year that changes. The Tar Heel State is often divided by narrow margins but did back Trump in each of his three presidential runs. However, Democrats are hopeful that their candidate, former Governor Roy Cooper, is in a strong position as a popular former statewide official. Republicans are running Michael Whatley, the former chair of the Republican National Committee (RNC). A Carolina Journal and Harper Polling survey showed Cooper up 13 points over Whatley, 52 percent to 39 percent. It surveyed 600 likely voters from August 9 to 10, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. An Elon University poll, meanwhile, showed Cooper up 11 points, 52 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 466 likely voters from July 23 to 31, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 5.6 percentage points. A poll from The New York Times and Siena University found Cooper up 7 points, 50 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 601 likely voters from June 15 to 27, 2026 with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. It’s considered a Lean Democratic race by the Cook Political Report. Ohio In Ohio, once a swing state that now leans Republican, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, is seeking a comeback after losing reelection in 2024. The special election is being held to fill the seat previously held by Vice President JD Vance. GOP Senator Jon Husted was appointed by Governor Mike Dewine as a temporary replacement and is also running for the remainder of the term. A Fox News poll showed Brown with an 8-point lead over Husted, 53 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 1,008 registered voters from August 6 to 10, 2026 with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. However, a poll from The New York Times and Siena University showed Husted up 3 points, 50 percent to 47 percent. It was conducted from June 15 to 28, 2026 among 601 likely voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4.7 percentage points. The Cook Political Report views the race as a toss-up. Texas Texas backed Trump by 14 points last year, but Democrats believe state Representative James Talarico will be competitive against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who has faced some scandals and an impeachment in the state’s GOP-led legislature. Donahue said Paxton is a particularly weak candidate in Texas. Another factor that will shape the Senate race is whether Latino voters, who shifted toward Trump in 2024, will revert back to Democrats, he said, pointing to concerns around inflation and the administration’s ramped up immigration policies that could shift the critical voting bloc. Growth in places such as the Dallas suburbs could also benefit Talarico, he said. An Emerson College poll showed Paxton with a single-point lead, 47 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 1,000 likely voters from August 9 to 10, 2026 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. Other recent polls have been more favorable to Talarico. A survey from Texas Southern University’s Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center showed Talarico up 2 points, 47 percent to 45 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters from July 27 to 30, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. The TexasPulse poll, conducted by ReconMR and the Texas A&M Bush School, gave Talarico a 4-point lead, 47 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 619 likely voters from July 27 to 30, 2026. The Cook Political Report classifies the race as Lean Republican. What Do Prediction Markets Show? Overall, prediction markets view the race for Senate control as roughly a toss-up. Kalshi gave the GOP a slight advantage with a 53 percent chance of winning a majority, while Polymarket gave Democrats a 51 percent chance of winning the majority. Democrats’ chances in the Senate have fluctuated over the past few months. At the start of the year, Republicans had a 67 percent chance of retaining Senate control, but that narrowed, with Kalshi showing a tied race in March, April and May. Democrats even were briefly favored in mid-April. However, over the past few weeks, Republicans’ chances have ticked up again. Here is a look at where key Senate races stand on Kalshi's markets. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. What Happens Next Polls will continue to be watched over the coming months to gauge the mood of the American electorate ahead of the midterms. Upcoming primaries in states such as New Hampshire may also shape the race for control of the Senate. Donahue said that over the coming months, it will be interesting to see whether any other states “creep into the battleground.” Republicans hope to make states such as Minnesota or New Hampshire more competitive though they currently lean toward Democrats. Meanwhile, Democrats may view Kansas as a “sleeper race.” He also noted that the Nebraska Senate race, where independent Dan Osborn is running against GOP Senator Pete Ricketts, could be another race to watch.
news.summary: Democrats and Republicans are engaged in a close race for control of the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, recent polls show.

news.title: NABJ went too far on Stephen A. Smith. He should still listen | Opinion
news.text:
Nothing quite stings like criticism from your own.

I know that as a journalist. I know it as a Black man. And after nearly 30 years as a Black journalist, I know what it feels like when those two worlds collide.

I’ve been fortunate to receive accolades and awards from both the journalism profession and the Black community. I’m grateful for them. But funny thing about praise: You can receive 1,000 compliments, and somehow it’s the one piece of criticism that follows you home.

Especially when it comes from people you respect.

That’s why I had some strong feelings when the National Association of Black Journalists gave ESPN personality and political commentator Stephen A. Smith one of its 2026 Thumbs Down Awards. NABJ says the award is intended for an individual or organization responsible for "especially insensitive, racist or stereotypical" coverage or commentary about the Black community, or practices contrary to the organization’s goals.

NABJ accused Smith of a recurring pattern of disparaging commentary toward prominent Black women in politics, sports and media. For example, Smith drew criticism after saying U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, whom he called an "educated, brilliant Black woman," was engaging in "verbiage and rhetoric for the streets" − language he later apologized for.

I think NABJ went too far. But I also think Smith is making a mistake if that’s the only message he takes from this.

Opinion: I felt bad for Stephen A. Smith. Then he clung to the legs of Black women

Stephen A. Smith doesn’t belong in this category

Let’s start with what shouldn’t be controversial: Stephen A. Smith is one of the most successful Black journalists and media personalities in America.

You don’t have to like him. You don’t have to agree with him. Lord knows I don’t always agree with him, particularly when he ventures from sports into politics.

But you can’t deny what he’s accomplished.

Smith has reached the top of an industry where Black journalists historically had to fight just to get into the room. He has also helped create opportunities for younger Black journalists and supported NABJ, including bringing ESPN’s highly rated "First Take" to its annual convention.

That context matters when you’re handing somebody a Thumbs Down Award.

NABJ’s own description says the distinction is intended to call attention to racist or stereotypical journalism and conduct contrary to the organization’s mission. Previous recipients have included news organizations criticized for newsroom cuts that disproportionately affected journalists of color.

That’s serious territory.

Smith can be bombastic. He can be abrasive. He can be over the top. That’s practically the business model. But treating him as though his body of work represents some fundamental betrayal of Black journalism doesn’t sit right with me.

Criticize the commentary? Absolutely.

Challenge his tone? Fair game.

Call out specific statements that NABJ believes unfairly demean Black women? Do it.

But there is a difference between holding one of our own accountable and branding him as an enemy of the values Black journalists have spent generations fighting to uphold.

I believe NABJ crossed that line.

I understand why Smith is angry. I’ve been there.

Smith didn’t exactly take the criticism quietly.

On his "Straight Shooter" show, he blasted NABJ’s leadership and questioned why nobody contacted him before publicly accusing him of disparaging Black women. He later took his grievances to Sean Hannity’s Fox News program, where he insisted he wouldn’t back down.

Not the route I would have taken. But I understand the emotion behind it. Getting slapped down by people you thought were down with you hurts differently. I learned that early in my career.

I participated in an Enquirer project that enraged parts of Cincinnati’s Black community. The criticism came hard and fast. I was accustomed to being the journalist who asked uncomfortable questions, put public officials in the hot seat, and demanded that others explain themselves. Suddenly, I was the one sweating beneath the interrogation lights.

And my first instinct? Defend myself.

Defend the story. Defend the decisions. Defend the journalism. Explain what people misunderstood. Explain what I intended. Basically, do everything except fully absorb what people were trying to tell me.

A mentor of mine who wasn’t a journalist finally cut through all of my explanations. “You messed up,” he told me. “You’ve got to live with that and do better.”

But I needed to hear it. It forced me to confront something journalists sometimes forget: Intent doesn’t erase impact.

I may not have intended to hurt or offend people. I may have believed the journalism was defensible. But if people in my own community were telling me that my work had harmed them, I owed them more than an argument. I owed them a listen. That lesson has stayed with me ever since.

Which brings me back to Stephen A. Smith.

Calling it like you see it doesn’t excuse how you say it

Smith says he’s heard NABJ’s criticism. The more important question is whether he’s actually listening.

Smith’s initial response has sounded much more like the younger version of me − busy defending himself, his intentions and his record − than someone seriously wrestling with what his peers are trying to tell him. That’s understandable. It’s also potentially a missed opportunity.

I make my living offering opinions. I understand the bullseye that comes with that. I frequently tell people that when I criticize a politician, public official, business leader, or community institution, it isn’t personal to me.

But I’ve learned something else over the years: It may not be personal to me. It’s usually personal to them.

I’m talking about their job performance. Their business. Their organization. Their reputation. Sometimes their family or people they love.

Words have weight. That’s especially true when you have a microphone as large as Stephen A. Smith’s.

No public figure should be immune from fair criticism because she’s a Black woman. Not Joy Reid. Not Michelle Obama. Not Jasmine Crockett. Not Kamala Harris.

And certainly not Stephen A. Smith. Or me.

Journalists and commentators aren’t supposed to make friends. As Stephen A. Smith said, we’re supposed to call balls and strikes as we see them. But that doesn’t absolve us from examining how we call them.

We can be tough without being demeaning. We can be provocative without being reckless. We can challenge someone’s ideas without diminishing the person. And when people whose judgment we respect tell us we’ve crossed that line, we should at least be willing to consider that they might see something we don’t.

Sometimes a thumbs down is an invitation to look inward

Today’s media landscape makes all of this harder. The lines separating journalism, opinion and entertainment have become increasingly blurred. Few people walk that line more visibly − or profitably − than Stephen A. Smith.

His job rewards volume. Conflict gets clicks. Outrage travels faster than nuance. The hotter the take, the farther it travels.

But I don’t believe Stephen A. Smith deserves to be treated as an enemy of Black journalism. And my disagreement with NABJ on this doesn’t diminish what the organization has meant to thousands of other Black journalists or me.

Organizations we value can get things wrong. So can journalists we respect.

Stephen A. Smith doesn’t have to agree with NABJ. He doesn’t have to apologize for opinions he still believes are right. And he certainly doesn’t have to stop calling it as he sees it.

But before he makes another television appearance explaining why everybody else is wrong, maybe he should consider the possibility that the people criticizing him aren’t trying to destroy him. Maybe they’re trying to tell him something.

I once had someone who cared enough about me to put it much more simply: You messed up. Live with it. Do better.

Sometimes the people closest to us deliver the criticism that stings the most. And sometimes that’s precisely why we need to listen.

Opinion and Engagement Editor Kevin S. Aldridge can be reached at kaldridge@enquirer.com. On X: @kevaldrid.

news.title: Kamala Harris’ Gen-Z-focused account on X takes swipe at Trump’s failed political endorsements
news.text:
Kamala Harris’ Gen-Z-focused social media page has taken a swipe at President Trump’s failed political endorsements.

​Harris, who was defeated by Trump after jumping into the presidential race back in 2024, launched her account, Headquarters, back in February.

​The account, which was repurposed from her previously campaign page KamalaHQ, regularly blasts the president over his public gaffes and policy decisions.

​On Wednesday, the Headquarters account hit out at the commander-in-chief again, this time highlighting all of the candidates who were endorsed by Trump this year - only to lose their primaries.

​Several Republican heavy hitters made the list, including embattled Representative Cory Mills - the incumbent in the race - who lost the Republican primary for Florida’s 7th District on Tuesday.

Representative ​Andy Ogles, who previously wrote on X that “Muslims don’t belong in American society,” also featured on the Headquarters list, having lost his House primary in Tennessee earlier in August.

​“Andy is a Conservative Warrior who has strong support from his Community,” Trump had written on Truth Social, referencing Ogles.

​Burt Jones and Pamela Evette, both sitting Lieutenant Governors running to become governors in their respective states, Georgia and South Carolina, also featured.

​Trump’s endorsement has long been highly coveted by Republican politicians, although, increasingly, cracks appear to be forming in his MAGA base.

​Former loyalist Marjorie Taylor Greene, who infamously broke with Trump over the Epstein files, wrote on X this week: “I can’t remember the last time I saw someone wearing a maga (sic) hat or Trump shirt.”

​Meanwhile, an analysis by The New York Times suggested that viewership of right-wing influencers’ accounts on YouTube, X, and Rumble has plummeted in recent months.

​Harris, who lost in a landslide to Trump, has continued to make public appearances since her defeat and even embarked on an international book tour promoting her tell-all book about the 2024 campaign, 107 Days.

​Harris has also consistently been a frontrunner in polls tracking who will become the next Democratic presidential candidate, but recently had one of her own endorsements in a U.S. Senate race dismissed.

​The former vice president had thrown her support behind Alaskan Mary Peltola, who would go on to win the Democratic Senate primary, last week.

​“If there’s anyone who can flip Alaska and secure the Senate majority for Democrats – it’s Mary,” an email sent to supporters and signed by Harris read.

​Peltola’s spokesperson later dismissed the endorsement in a statement handed to KTUU, using a term for the contiguous U.S.

​“Mary isn’t seeking endorsements from anyone from the Lower 48 – her focus is and always will be Alaska,” the spokesperson said.

​Nate Adams, the spokesperson for Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, hit out at the endorsement in a statement given to The Guardian.

​“Kamala Harris supported the Biden administration’s disastrous anti-Alaska agenda, which is why Alaskans rejected her by double digits,” the statement read.

news.summary: Kamala Harris repurposed her campaign account into a Gen-Z focused page that takes aim at President Trump’s gaffes and policies
